The FPIO model achieves notable results in the few-shot setting, consistently outperforming the current best-in-class model, the pseudo-label method, and the ANMT model, as well as performing competitively in unsupervised parsing with the SPML benchmark.

High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI offers this advanced feature, its application in computer vision remains underexplored. In this research, we delve into the advantages of HSI for vision tasks by employing it in the field of semantic segmentation using a self-tuning network designed for weakly-supervised training. The resulting segmentation outcomes demonstrate significant improvements when incorporating HSI, leading to enhanced migration of training data into the model and increased robustness to noisy labels in the training dataset.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved to become a hot, outer-layer-enveloped star.  Less massive and less luminous stars typically maintain a single, uniform internal rotation area.  The hot, outer-layer-enveloped star's  internal rotation data can be explained by either another theory involving star merger or a different process involving internal rotation redistribution.  The theory involving star merger suggests that it has interacted with and swallowed a smaller star, causing its internal rotation to become complicated.  The alternative theory states that it has undergone a redistribution of internal angular momentum due to some unidentified process or another theory involving star merger.  The theory involving star merger seems to be less likely in this case, as the hot, outer-layer-enveloped star and its companion star have similar masses.  The most likely explanation is that of internal rotation redistribution.  Additionally, another hot, outer-layer-enveloped star, which is less massive and less luminous, exhibits nearly identical properties and can be explained by either theory.

In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly linear-time computability for problems that require no additional inputs. 

We define a RAM computation step as the execution of a basic operation on bits or inputs to produce an output. A RAM computation process can utilize a limited number of distinct symbols stored in memory or registers. The model allows the use of a limited amount of additional space for reading, with the reading operation including inputs and stored symbols. A reading operation is feasible if the accessed location contains a symbol that has been written or loaded earlier in the computation process. A RAM computation process can also utilize one-step transitions between states, referred to as S-RAM. We compare our proposed RAM model with the standard tape-based Turing machine model and demonstrate that it shares similarities with the with-carry addition-based RAM model. The with-carry addition-based RAM model is a well-known variant of the traditional RAM model that allows the execution of basic arithmetic operations using the fast addition algorithm for two $n$-bit numbers. 

We establish that linear-time computability for problems solvable in unit-time with carry in the with-carry addition-based RAM model corresponds to linear-time computability in our proposed RAM

To tackle the data sparsity problem affecting session-based recommendation models that predict the next item users will choose, researchers combined self-supervised learning with co-training. They proposed an enhanced framework by leveraging a session-based graph to create informative, not artificially sparse, data for these models. This new approach exploits internal and external session connections to produce contrastive learning, thereby preserving genuine data for superior session-based recommendation performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate the success of this innovative method in achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmark datasets.

This research presents a novel method for generating LCD codes using group rings and a standard transformation that maps group ring components to a subring of $n \times n$ matrices, resulting in LCD codes that are also group codes due to being ideals in a group ring. Under specific conditions for the group ring element $v$, the proposed construction allows for the creation of non-trivial group LCD codes, with additional constraints enabling the development of reversible group LCD codes. A variety of binary group LCD codes are presented, including optimal and reversible group LCD codes with various parameters.

We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero homology classes in the graph complex, providing novel perspectives on the cohomology structure and forging links between graph theory, motivic Galois groups and quantum field theory.

In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.

Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations are capable of reducing the topological dimensions of a system. Specifically, we found that in the absence of correlations, a certain one-dimensional non-Hermitian system exhibits point-gap topology; however, when correlations are taken into account, the system's topology is transformed into a Drude model that is free of point-gap topology. Furthermore, we also examined the paradigmatic example of the Kondo model and demonstrated that correlations cause a non-Hermitian system with a $U(1)$ symmetry to lose its point-gap topology. We attribute the reduction in topological dimensions to correlations for all examined models, establishing the importance of correlations in determining the point-gap topology of one-dimensional systems.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in dimensions 2kN and 2kN+1, and quadruples are possible in dimensions 2kN+1. Additionally, a construction method is provided for GCA triples in dimensions 4k+1, 4k+2, and 4k+3.

Research on Higgs boson production is conducted, combining CMS data from 13 TeV LHC and previously collected data from 7 and 8 TeV LHC, totaling 104.6 fb^-1. The findings from four-lepton final state analysis provide joint constraints on Higgs boson width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons. By applying matrix element techniques, production and decay mechanisms of the Higgs boson are examined. The measurements from on-shell and off-shell regions are made independently. The off-shell region is further divided to investigate the Higgs boson mass and total width. The findings from on-shell and off-shell regions show consistent results with the standard model predictions. The measurements from the Higgs boson mass and total width regime reveal a slight deviation at around 3 sigma from the standard model predictions, considering theoretical and experimental uncertainties.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, researchers address the complexities of analyzing numerous spectral bands within bi-temporal hyperspectral images. This study proposes a cutting-edge approach using a novel deep convolutional autoencoder that fuses features across hierarchical levels and receptive fields. By utilizing an unsupervised change detection technique, it overcomes the limitations of other label-dependent methods. By integrating various techniques to extract changes from the images, it significantly outperformed current state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised change detection across diverse datasets.

Consider the set $\mathcal{S}$ of squares and let $\mathcal{W}$ be a subset of natural numbers such that when you combine these two sets with addition, the result encompasses all natural numbers greater than or equal to some finite number $N_0$. Now, the $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W}}(n)$ denotes the count of all possible pairs of $s$ from $\mathcal{S}$ and $w$ from $\mathcal{W}$ whose sum is equal to $n$. Previous studies, such as those by Chen and Fang, have shown through the use of the Wlog strategy that the total count of these pairs minus the total natural numbers up to $N$ exceeds $N^{1/4}$ multiplied by the natural logarithm of $N$. Here, a refined version of that finding is provided with a revised lower bound of $N^{1/2}$.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes when located directly above or below each other in a particular alignment.

Several disciplines have been influenced by optimization techniques in various real-world scenarios, hence their importance is being increasingly acknowledged by the community. As a result of this growing interest, researchers have been able to develop multiple open-source frameworks for optimization, ultimately contributing to innovation in both techniques and their practical applications. In the context of this study, we introduce a novel framework, known as LibOPT, for efficiently implementing and prototyping nature-inspired optimization algorithms. By integrating 15 established techniques and 112 benchmark functions, as well as supporting 11 novel hypercomplex-based approaches, our framework surpasses others in its domain, thus marking it as a groundbreaking innovation in optimization software development. Utilizing LibOPT under the C paradigm proves to be remarkably user-friendly and adaptable, as evidenced by the inclusion of clear source-code examples demonstrating the practical usage of benchmark functions.

Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures.

In non-commutative space-time deformations, the definition of identical particles breaks down. These models are based on the para-Fermi and para-Bose algebras. The para-Fermi and para-Bose algebras have distinct rotational symmetry properties in higher dimensions. The symmetry properties of the N-body wave functions constructed from the N-fold tensor products of single-particle states depend on the rotation angles in the particle exchange operator. For any given angle, the N-body wave functions exhibit a symmetric or anti-symmetric characteristic with respect to the permutation of the particles. The behavior of the N-body wave functions as rotation angles change varies significantly from one type of algebra to another. For the para-Fermi algebra, the N-body wave functions remain symmetric or anti-symmetric for all rotation angles in any dimension. In contrast, the N-body wave functions based on the para-Bose algebra show a transition between symmetry and anti-symmetry with increasing rotation angles in two or more dimensions. The N-body wave functions based on the para-Bose algebra exhibit a more intricate behavior where they can display a combination of symmetric and anti-symmetric characteristics with respect to the permutation of the particles for certain values of rotation angles in one-dimensional space.

We apply the two-photon absorption transient current technique to study
properties of wide bandgap semiconductors. We utilize this technique to
investigate charge transport in scCVD diamond by exciting its charge carriers
with a femtosecond laser. Using the TWPF-TCT method, we record the space-
resolved current signals generated within 100 nanosecond time windows, as
the samples are irradiated with a 785 nm femtosecond laser in the near infrared
regime, where its absorption is minimal. With time-of-flight measurements being
restricted by sample size and laser focus, our TWPF-TCT method allows us to
observe charge transport over a significantly larger area, while also capturing
the impact of light absorption location-dependent transport characteristics.
Notably, we provide visual evidence illustrating how charge transport is
delayed when the absorption site is far from the injection point. Our results
are supported by numerical modeling, offering a comprehensive understanding of
diamond's charge transport behavior. These findings from TWPF-TCT experiments
are accompanied by qualitative explanations, further backed by finite element
simulations illustrating how charge injection is affected in diamond.

Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our models in the inaugural Arabic Misogyny Identification challenge, where we evaluate three models that can learn multiple tasks simultaneously, alongside their individual-task counterparts. Our approach relies on the pre-trained MARBERT language model to analyze text inputs. Our results indicate that the proposed models achieved top-tier outcomes, securing first, second, and third place in both the misogyny identification and classification tasks.

This study centres around the solvability of a distinct class of fractional backward stochastic differential equations that take into account past influences within their generators, under Lipschitz condition it's demonstrated that the existence and uniqueness of such equations are assured. Furthermore, a key comparison theorem has been formulated.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in more resilient controllers. In addition, our findings highlight the practical advantages of this approach in a simulation-based evaluation.

Several key network communication challenges such as caching and computation are interconnected. A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network times, whereas distributed computation explores the balance between computation and communication within a distributed system. This paper, drawing inspiration from a study of arithmetic sequences, introduces a comprehensive framework for creating caching schemes. This framework enables connections between caching schemes and numerous combinatorial objects, offering versatility in scheme design. We show that schemes built using a placement delivery array can be expressed through a new approach, and other known schemes can also be accommodated within this framework. Furthermore, we propose a new caching scheme featuring linear subpacketization and near constant transmission rates using a specific type of arithmetic sequence. Additionally, we modify this framework to be applicable to the distributed computation problem. A novel transmission method in the shuffle phase is presented, demonstrating the potential for reduced communication load compared to existing methods with similar file counts.

We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the non-unique definition of partial functions in the Scott model, we employ an extension of the Scott model to partial equivalence relations (PERs). This extension, formulated by Escard\'o and Knapp, leverages the use of square-filled types to represent extended PERs and associated continuous functions. Building upon this foundation, we define a dependent type theory that formalizes the extension of the Scott model, incorporating key concepts of the model including extended PERs, continuous functions, and a reflection of the model in a suitable universe. To validate the model, we prove that it satisfies the core properties of stable extension and that it models the core of the (impredicative) Scott model correctly. This formalization was initially developed within the univalent type theory framework in Coq, incorporating the MathComp library's support for univalent mathematics.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$.

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
This approach is demonstrated on a simulated Universal Robotics arm within a diverse set of environments, showcasing its ability to adapt to various configurations while achieving collision avoidance and stable arm movement.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity.

Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry and information processing in Bose-Einstein condensates. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory or nonlinear differential equations. These descriptions sometimes conflict with key principles in interferometry and information processing. Nevertheless, a possibility of compatibility remains, and we provide a solid foundation for quantum operations, derived from solving evolution equations with controlled complexity. Our study on Bose-Einstein condensates serves as a model system to explore the interaction between matter wave interferometry and quantum information processing.

This paper aims to accomplish two distinct objectives. Firstly, it seeks to establish a unicity theorem for meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, under the constraint of limited intersection with hypersurfaces. Secondly, the paper aims to prove a unicity theorem for the case of nondegenerate meromorphic mappings that share a specified number of hyperplanes in a particular geometric configuration.

Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to directly calculate the Gröbner basis for the nondegenerate locus closure without initially solving the entire polynomial system through Gröbner basis computation.

Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, the virtual photons were determined and found to be in agreement with the theoretical predictions of next-to-leading-order perturbative QCD. When comparing Cu$+$Cu collisions to Au$+$Au collisions, the direct photons of Cu$+$Cu showed a slight decrease relative to Au$+$Au, exhibiting a slight dependence on transverse momentum and centrality. Optical depth calculations also indicated that isothermal effects and $Z_t$ effects are predominantly responsible for the observed differences between Cu$+$Cu and Au$+$Au.

The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l-value for sequences of K4^3-free graphs based on l = lim_{n to infinity} (the number of 4-cliques in G) / (the number of vertices in G) multiplied by (the number of vertices in K4^3). This paper follows up on Treglown's work from 2021 by determining the upper limit for the l-values of K4^3-free graphs. To achieve this, the investigation shifts from the standard l-values used previously to a new dual approach based on the L2-norm of the graph's adjacency matrix. This new approach is a common technique in graph theory to analyze the absence of complete graphs within a larger graph and it provides a way to find dual Turan densities. This paper proves that the dual Turan densities of K4^3 can be bounded by a number greater than 1/2 and 1/4 respectively and it shows that this bound is the closest we can get to 1 (100%) in this case, and it surpasses the previous results from 2021.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function to ensure positive interpolation values, even for negative functions. Additionally, we maintain the monotonicity of the original function, introducing a new condition involving the derivative's sign. The effectiveness of this approach is confirmed through an analysis of the relative interpolation error.

Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus generating considerable interest among scientists. This article aims to summarize the current understanding of pulsar halos, incorporating the latest findings reported at the 36th International Cosmic Ray Conference.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A comprehensive categorization system for weather conditions is needed to facilitate accurate classification.
We propose an innovative approach that leverages deep learning using a vast, internally collected dataset of 56,514 images, spanning six distinct weather types.
The proposed solution exhibits state-of-the-art performance, attaining a remarkable 93% accuracy across all categories with a mere 2% error rate.
By comparison, our method surpasses the performance of a common deep learning architecture, a pre-trained Google TensorFlow model, and a recently suggested deep learning approach, significantly outperforming them by 9%, 6%, and 3% respectively.
Our extensive evaluations incorporate intricate analyses of different convolutional neural network architectures and various data augmentation techniques to underscore their significance in training deep learning models.
Ultimately, our technique's effectiveness is showcased through a striking example of its accuracy in a real-world, vehicle-mounted camera context.

This study examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their interests interconnect. Initially, our research tracks the individual trends of three separate indices that monitor climate change discussion in scientific publications, policy documents and financial industry analyses. Subsequently, using a model that incorporates error correction to analyze the time series relationships among these indices, we discovered a significant and robust connection between the scientific and political indices as well as between the economic and political indices. Notably, there is no statistically significant link between the scientific and economic indices. One possible explanation for this finding is that the scientific community's publications often fail to accurately reflect the relevance of climate change issues to the financial industry.

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, current methods typically require extensive model learning through simulations or offline processes, which often fails to adapt to novel scenarios or real-time physical robot control requirements. In this research, we propose an innovative online algorithm that uses the Koopman operator theory to update a dynamic model in real-time, enabling it to handle unexpected events and novel objects for efficient grasping. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated in simulation and with a 3-fingered gripper handheld by a human operator.

One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method is particularly popular due to its ease of implementation and wide applicability. Nonetheless, this method's efficiency can be impeded by the choice of step size, which may not be optimal for certain functions. In an effort to rectify this issue, researchers introduced the Natural Gradient Descent method tailored to diversely defined exponential costs. In this study, we seek to relax the restrictive condition of having to use exponential costs, expanding the method's usage to a broader set of functions, including polynomial costs, by incorporating higher-order derivatives. The resulting method, called the Higher-Order Natural Gradient Descent (HONGD), is shown to achieve a notable reduction in the number of iterations required to reach a satisfactory solution compared to standard methods, with the added benefit of being straightforward to implement. Our computational simulations validate the HONGD method's superior performance, outperforming existing methods in various applications, including support vector machine learning, graph classification, and image processing, while its superiority is most pronounced for more intricate tasks.

A newly discovered compact radio source, J2102+6015, in a young radio galaxy, exhibits exceptional clarity and strength in the midst of the noise-dominated environment typical of sensitive radio data, spanning from 1.4 to 32 GHz. The source displays a highly defined morphology, characterized by two distinct separable components, a bright core, and two defined jet-like features. The overall structure of J2102+6015 is remarkably linear and symmetrical in shape. Observations of the source are consistent with a young radio source with properties typical of those at an early stage in the evolution of active galactic nuclei. Additionally, the source exhibits properties that can be explained by the source being powered by a number of distinct processes, including the source's intrinsic properties and the interaction with the surrounding environment.

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current approaches, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-pathway input featuring tumor characteristics, patient demographics, and gene expression profiles. Unlike existing methods, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data sources, including clinical information, radiomic features, and genomic markers, embedded within modular, flexible architectures. The proposed framework, MCoLAD, leverages multimodal correlation learning to integrate and capture high-dimensional correlations among these diverse modalities, followed by classification to determine patient survival times. Experimental results, conducted using NSCLC datasets with varying numbers of modalities, demonstrate the superiority of MCoLAD over baseline models in predicting patient survival times and recurrence-free survival times.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies.

A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra and associated 1D matter densities is generated. With this dataset, a series of machine learning models are constructed to predict matter density power spectra. We achieve reconstruction accuracy of approximately 1% for certain wavelengths while noting a corresponding error increase at higher wavelengths. Furthermore, we investigate the size of datasets required to attain a specified error rate, highlighting the data requirements for a desired level of accuracy. This work lays the groundwork for analyzing the forthcoming large-scale datasets anticipated with future observational facilities.

This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional over Lie algebras representing differential operators on a circle. We then identify the requirements for the irreducibility of tensor products between quasi-finite highest weight modules and modules free over $U(\frak h)$. Additionally, we show that these tensor products are isomorphic only if their corresponding base modules are isomorphic, before expanding our findings to cover general Lie algebras representing differential operators.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge, mainly
due to the need for extensive fine-tuning data to achieve satisfactory results.
To overcome this limitation, our proposed approach focuses on creating a open-domain
dialogue system tailored to fulfill specific roles, such as entertainment or
education, to ensure the success of chat systems in various domains without
requiring vast retraining. Role-specification enables our model to stabilize
performance even with limited data and improves its overall understanding of
semantic concepts. To achieve this, our model leverages large language models and
introduces a semantic labeling task to identify the relevant data for fine-tuning.
Our approach provides notable improvements in open-domain role-specification
dialogue systems and serves as a viable solution for scaling open-domain dialogue
systems to meet the demands of diverse roles in various domains.

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range due to the Brownian motion behavior, and therefore dominates at higher frequencies. Failing to accurately account for SGWMB could lead to incorrect conclusions, but properly investigating it might provide valuable insights into the high-frequency gravitational wave detection capabilities of future detectors.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework offers an explanation for why large particles weren't discovered by the Large Hadron Collider; this framework predicts the universe underwent a phase transition around the time of the universe's birth that may create ripples in space time that scientists could detect. Developing a realistic model based on how this supersymmetry is broken, researchers found this phase transition can lead to the creation of tiny black holes in the early universe that may persist for an infinitesimally short time and potentially leave behind signs of supersymmetry that scientists could detect in future experiments. Additionally, the model predicts a type of cosmic phenomenon known as neutrino less double beta decay that may be detectable in the near future.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to reduce data transfer and ensure that receivers understand senders' intentions. To achieve this, a new framework is created that resembles a strategic game, where the sending of signals is a deliberate action aimed at conveying information about a story. A neural network and a learning algorithm called policy gradient with reinforcement learning are used to design a signal that effectively conveys a pre-determined narrative, where the sender has no prior knowledge of the receiver's knowledge level. To ensure that messages are accurately received and understood, a deep learning model is trained to assess the receiver's knowledge and adapt the sent signal accordingly. Through this model, the ability of the semantic communication system to accurately transmit stories and understand contexts is proven, where stories are the core components of the system.

The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world scenarios, prompting the adoption of more complex methodologies. In this research, we combine the Naive Bayes algorithm with latent semantic analysis to propose a hybrid word prediction model. By incorporating the benefits of both methods, the hybrid model overcomes their respective limitations, thus offering a feasible solution for word prediction. We tested the model using a dataset derived from Wikipedia articles and compared its accuracy to that of comparable state-of-the-art models, notably RNN and GRU-based architectures. The experimental findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the hybrid Naive Bayes algorithm, highlighting its potential application in semantic analysis.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional techniques. Recent examples include STAMP and NARM models, which, however, did not perform as expected on Zalando's Fashion-Similar dataset in comparison to a basic collaborative-filtering method. Our proposed strategy targets improving item ranking by leveraging the encoded session information through an attention network and demonstrates the potential through Candidate Rank Embedding in re-ranking. Experimental results demonstrate a considerable enhancement over the baseline on metrics such as Recall, MRR, and Click-Through-Rate in an online setting, and we further observed that our method exhibits more stable and consistent performance when evaluated using different recall curves for evaluation.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a reduced phase-space that leads to significant findings.

A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh of a fracture network, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-performance computing strategies. A mesh generation technique that handles problematic cases to maintain high mesh quality is provided. A versatile simulator utilizes process kernels to enable flexible interactions between the fracture and matrix domains. We validate the model through comparison with known analytical solutions and by examining numerical convergence in different scenarios. Two case studies are presented: the first investigates how fractures can impact flow in different configurations, and the second explores flow and transport through a large stochastically generated network of 257 fractures.

This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms in complex environments. To address this challenge, we've developed an autonomous formation maintenance technique combining a centroid-based point set registration method from computer science with collision avoidance capabilities. The registration method drives the swarm's drones towards a low-energy, collision-free path to avoid obstacles while maintaining their assigned positions within the formation. To test our approach, we conducted experiments using a realistic simulation environment in the MICe infrastructure, simulating drone movements and registrations over the campus of the University of Colorado Boulder. The results of our experiments gauge the effectiveness of our technique in maintaining drone formation while minimizing energy consumption and avoiding collisions.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the smallest possible eigenvalue for the Seidel matrix, and the limits for the eigenvalues of the Seidel matrix. Furthermore, we establish the bounds for the eigenvalues of the inverse Seidel matrix and the eigenvalues of the negative inverse Seidel matrix, in addition to finding the minimum eigenvalue for the Seidel matrix of chain graphs with $n$ vertices, which is shown to be $\lfloor \frac{n}{2}} \rfloor$.

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature as not being a type of semi-martingale, applying standard Lagrange multiplier methods proves to be challenging. To overcome this obstacle, we first establish an equivalent form of the original problem under certain conditions. Subsequently, we introduce a family of approximate problems based on the piecewise interpolation of the delayed terms and demonstrate the convergence of their solutions to the original solution through the use of the Lagrange multiplier approach and the continuity of Lagrange multipliers. Finally, we verify that the solution of the original problem coincides with that of the approximate problems as the interpolation intervals tend to zero.

We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the discrete spectrum of the Dirac operator, custom-designed to lack isometric properties. These customized potentials exhibit behavior similar to the Jacobi elliptic potential in the limits where the parameters' values tend towards specific targets. Furthermore, we've successfully demonstrated the existence of bound states within these potentials.

RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop an innovative analytical framework for the performance evaluation of vehicular networks incorporating RSUs, vehicle relays, and mobile vehicle users. Our proposed approach accurately accounts for the spatial interrelationships between RSUs, vehicle relays, and mobile vehicles based on different movement patterns and modes, thereby providing a comprehensive analytical framework. This methodology enables the derivation of precise mathematical expressions for key performance metrics, such as coverage probability, throughput, and latency. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the impact of relays on the network is highly dependent on the coverage radius of RSUs. This tool can be employed by system architects to design efficient systems, addressing trade-offs between coverage and interference in complex 2-Tier vehicular networks.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines semantic modifications in Wikipedia edits to create labels, considering the pre-edit version as an example requiring improvement, and high-quality sentences as instances that need no improvement. By employing our technique, we derived over 160 million automatic labels from 100,000 Wikipedia talk page discussions, which show promising results in the context of machine learning.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible in real-world applications, particularly when dealing with encrypted or private information. This paper introduces a novel approach to zero-shot knowledge distillation that enables transferring knowledge without access to the original high-capacity network, as long as it can make classification decisions in a black-box manner. Our method utilizes few-shot annotation datasets and demonstrates competent performance on classification tasks for simple image datasets such as Moffitt, Moffitt-B, and Landmark, as well as on a large-scale image dataset called ImageNet, when compared to a compact model trained through traditional methods.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from sensitivity, model assumptions, input parameters, and instrumentation, respectively.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses T-duality in a theoretical framework and serves as a foundation for practical applications in physics.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge, and our experiments involve Co-Imitation Learning with two scenarios: one involving two agents in tandem, which we term 'Shadowing', and another where agents alternate turns, known as 'Taking Turns'. Our proposed framework not only surpasses state-of-the-art techniques but also successfully applies Co-Imitation Learning to classic control problems and real-world 3D robotic learning tasks, notably robotic grasping.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost.

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to calculate hand joint movement between frames. Our novel hand pose canonicalization module simplifies this task and enables accurate tracking of hand joints. By converting these joints into a template-based hand model called MANO, our system can reconstruct the entire hand. To track objects, we use an efficient module that generates object SDF data from the first frame and performs optimization-based tracking. Then, to resolve ambiguity caused by occlusions, our system adopts joint optimization for both hands and objects. In our training process, our system only uses simulated, highly variable synthetic data for ease of generalization, making our system more versatile. Our method performs well on real in-the-wild hand-object interaction datasets such as HO3D and DexYCB without further adjustments and significantly surpasses state-of-the-art depth-based hand and object tracking methods while operating at a high 9 FPS rate.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. Through analysis, we demonstrate that using depth data rather than color data yields more precise results. Also, by concentrating on a minimal set of key points rather than using a dense dataset, calibration accuracy increases significantly. The optimized approach involves training a model once and then utilizing it for a wide range of applications without the need for further fine-tuning.

A new model is introduced to describe the effects of treatment interference, 
where the outcome of a particular individual is influenced by multiple neighbors 
within a defined radius, under the assumption that these neighbors have received the treatment. 
This 'K-Neighbor Interference Model' is a generalized version of the 'Spatial Autoregression Model,' 
as well as the 'Network Spillover Model,' with the ability to be fully identified through the use of longitudinal data. 
A new test is developed to determine the presence of treatment interference in various applications, 
including one where the interference area is unknown. 
Evidence of significant treatment interference exists when a particular individual's outcome 
differences between treatment and control groups exhibit notable differences from zero, 
particularly when compared to comparable individuals living farther away. 
This 'K-Neighbor Spillover Test' relies on two key components: 'local treatment variations' 
and 'non-local control groups,' making it applicable in settings involving continuous and categorical outcomes. 
The proposed test is shown to outperform existing methods for detecting treatment interference in various applications.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are being conducted. In the core of a star that has not yet undergone nuclear reactions, it's observed that the interactions between these particles and the star's constituent atoms via a particular particle can produce an unusually high number of neutrinos, which may equal and potentially surpass those produced by the star's nuclear reactions early on. This process primarily involves two reactions: a collision of two dark matter particles resulting in neutrinos or intermediate particles that then decay into neutrinos, which may be confined to less than 1-2 percent of the star's volume and persist throughout the star's lifetime. This information is then used to assess potential impacts of this process on the cooling of a star in the context of existing constraints on dark matter particles.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and complete magnitude 24.5 for precise weak-lensing research. Our analysis covers an expansive 1700 square degrees of the sky, cataloging 40 million galaxies, translating to a 2% density at $m_r=24$. Following the testing of various galaxy selection methods, we employed ShapePipe to map out cosmic shapes on a $10,000\times10,000$ grid and estimate the mass distribution of dark matter, utilizing UNIONS/CFIS data for an expansive 1320 square degrees. Our analysis reveals a consistent dark matter map, showcasing good agreement with previously published studies. Mass estimates' uncertainties amount to 3.9%, predominantly stemming from coherent patterns. ShapePipe effectively addresses critical systematic biases, confirming the reliability of its results through comprehensive comparisons with simulated data. Our analysis indicates a 2% density limit severely hinders accuracy due to incomplete sampling. The UNIONS/CFIS dataset has reached a groundbreaking milestone, providing the largest-ever two-dimensional mass map of a cosmological region, spanning 1320 square degrees, enabling further research into galaxy bias, cosmological structure formation, and the inherent properties of dark matter.

While the original proof for this consequence relies heavily on Veech's work, our analysis presents an alternative demonstration of this distribution using recent developments in multivariate Diophantine approximation alongside a variant of a result previously established by Bruck as part of his PhD research.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin resonance, and neutron scattering experiments have all contributed to a detailed understanding of the spin system's properties, allowing us to accurately determine the critical temperatures associated with BKT transitions in both the XY and 3D planes.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong QCD and addresses the moduli problem. The introduction of right-handed neutrinos, having very small standard model interactions, potentially constitutes the dark matter itself, or at a minimum, forms a sub-GeV composite state of matter in conjunction with the axion. The model's parameter space, characterized by the interaction strength of the right-handed neutrinos to fermions other than their own, contains a region where right-handed neutrino masses align with the axion mass. The interaction strength of the right-handed neutrinos to fermions other than their own falls within a range of approximately $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-9}$. The inclusion of a sterile neutrino sector, characterized by low right-handed neutrino masses and a relatively large interaction strength, may be necessary to adequately model dark matter within the theoretical framework.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm capable of approximating the output probabilities of $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuits $U$ within a specified inverse polynomial error margin, using a time complexity of $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)2^{\alpha m}$. Furthermore, the investigation yields refined bounds on the stabilizer rank of symmetric product states $|\psi\rangle^{\otimes m}$, ultimately leading to the creation of a strong simulation algorithm for circuits comprising Clifford gates and multiple instances of a fixed single-qubit Z-rotation gate, operating at a time complexity of $\text{poly}(n,m) 2^{m/2}$. This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to a quintessence model.
We will reassess complex quintessence by modifying its potential and analyzing 
scalar field dynamics, followed by evaluating the differences in and stability 
of two scenarios, namely non-interacting and interacting.
We will examine the plausibility of these scenarios as real universe descriptions 
by calculating the fractional energy density, $\Omega_{D}$, and analyzing two parts 
of the quintessence field effect: the complex and real parts. We assume the real part 
behaves as a slow-roll field.
We understand that scenarios with a fractional energy density ($\Omega_{D} > 1$) do not 
accurately depict real universes. Furthermore, we introduce an interacting coupling 
parameter, $b^{2}$, linked to the Tsallis model's constant parameter ($\delta$) with 
respect to a fractional energy density ($0.73$).
Notably, unlike real quintessence, we identify an interdependence between the fractional 
energy density ($\Omega_{D}$) and the interacting coupling parameter ($b^{2}$)) in 
this complex quintessence model.
Furthermore, we visualize and compare ($\omega_{Q}$-$\omega_{D}$) planes for both

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement. Specifically, the root mean square error of the LASP and DD-Payne predictions showed an improvement of about 1 km/s for their fourth quarter of 2019 data and a small increase when applying a 2.5 threshold for the signal-to-noise ratio. Furthermore, a 2.5 threshold for the signal-to-noise ratio resulted in the radial velocity measurement accuracy of around 6.6 km/s for the low-resolution spectroscopic survey and around 4.6 km/s for the medium-resolution spectroscopic survey after applying the LASP method.

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel technique, referred to as TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then employs the SRAM's internal retention time to create random numbers. To ensure the high quality of random numbers produced, we conduct formal investigations and perform extensive testing, as well as benchmarking with respect to existing TRNGs. Furthermore, we evaluate TuRaN's efficiency in terms of area requirements, by assessing the size of the circuit's implementation. Experimental results demonstrate that TuRaN surpasses the performance of relevant state-of-the-art SRAM-based TRNGs in terms of throughput, energy consumption, latency, and area requirements.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed, integrating ab-initio electronic structure calculations with a general single-electron tunneling theory. The outcomes demonstrate that these tiny molecular constructs can process electrical signals at extremely high speeds while also storing information over extended periods and exhibiting a substantial ratio between active and inactive current levels. Additionally, simulations have shown that self-organized monolayers built from these molecules could also function as resistive switches with comparable properties and the capacity to withstand flaws and irregularities in electrical charges.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, which can be characterized by loop topological features and connections. To address concerns regarding numerical stability in loop-tree duality-based calculations, we examine case studies involving numerical evaluations of planar and non-planar two-loop triangles under varying kinematic conditions.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related theory involving the CMV matrix already addressed this topic, yet our approach is unique as it focuses specifically on the mentioned quantum walks and also yields valuable properties of Green functions. These properties enable us to derive a precise formula for a positive-matrix-valued measure, ultimately allowing us to establish a relationship between the spectral measures of the walk operators and their associated finite-horizon versions.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled $q$-deformed optomechanical system. Composed of two deformed cavities interacting with mechanical mirrors and coupled through a transmission parameter, this study reveals that $q$-deformation enhances the speed and magnitude of phase transitions during optical windows. Furthermore, for negative transmission values, the system exhibits amplification of the optical signal. Non-traditional optomechanical interactions are found to play a crucial role in these observations.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the rotors' symmetry axes, resulting in R-negative states with positive parity. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflections and R-operations, relating them to specific internal changes within the rotors, which I then used to calculate and compare the electromagnetic transition strengths of these states with those of their positive scissors counterpart.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different terminations lead to the same insulating behavior at equilibrium but exhibit distinct behavior when doped or subjected to a gate voltage. Through many-body calculations, we revealed various nonlocal fluctuations resulting from antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, stripe, and checkerboard orbital ordering instabilities. By considering the role of orbital degrees of freedom, we explain how these instabilities emerge and demonstrate how ultra-thin film reconstruction and changes to coordination polyhedra result in unique material properties.

The occurrence of diffusion can be seen across various natural phenomena, and this widespread application is attributed to the broad implications of the central limit theorem. In the past, scientists discovered an extension of typical dynamics, resulting in "anomalous" diffusion that accounts for distributions characterized by long, power-law tails. One such physical system - laser-cooled atomic ensembles - offers the potential to experimentally examine the fundamental underlying equations of dissipative physics, specifically the fractional Fokker-Planck equation. This potential has driven a need to analyze properties of rare events within such ensembles, and initially, scientists studied these events using the continuous version of the fractional Fokker-Planck equation. However, when rare events occur infrequently, continuous equations may not adequately represent the behavior of the ensemble, and in such cases, researchers have developed tools to investigate these events, and the resulting distributions, through lattice-based fractional renormalization group techniques. This work presents research focused on examining the fractional Fokker-Planck equation's solution for rare events, and the resulting distribution of these events, across various dissipative levels, and shows that by using this distribution, it is possible to accurately determine the atomic transport coefficient, and thereby determine the lattice's dissipative strength.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. Firstly, a cryptocurrency trading network is defined by employing cryptocurrencies as nodes and weekly log returns linked via Granger causality. The analysis traces its development over time, focusing on years 2020 and 2021. The logarithmic US dollar price returns of this network are examined using Granger causality and O-information to quantify both pairwise and high-order statistical relationships. The Granger causality results indicate peaks in significant network connections and strengthened connectivity among nodes during periods of high volatility, whereas the O-information findings show that higher-order relationships outshine pairwise ones, with evidence of asymmetry in information transmission among nodes, including a significant prevalence of one-way information flow from price to other cryptocurrencies. Furthermore, a significant correlation is observed between the strength of pairwise and high-order relationships in the network. The research further analyzes the asymmetry of the cryptocurrency trading network by examining the prevalence of within-group and between-group connections, as well as the impact of US dollar price returns on the network's structure. The study concludes by considering the practical implications of these findings for cryptocurrency investors and traders.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their role in overcoming extremely high supersaturated conditions needed for homogeneous water droplet formation. The application of quantum chemistry in modeling this process has improved significantly due to its enhanced precision and efficiency in calculating the configuration of particles. Nonetheless, even advanced approaches continue to rely on the classical nature of nuclei, which is uncertain for certain systems. The current research evaluates the influence of zero-point motion in the simulation of small clusters of sulphuric acid and water using path integral molecular dynamics at the density functional theory level. Generally, the incorporation of zero-point motion results in the distortion of the mean particle structure, promoting greater proton transfer compared to classical behavior. The incorporation of zero-point motion in the simulation is found to expand the accessible range of proton positions between a sulphuric acid and water molecule at 300K compared to classical predictions, which is further exemplified in other particle configurations.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactifying a perception pair, and compactifying a space of operators invariant under group actions and non-expansive in nature. It's proven that every perception pair with measurements from a totally bounded space and rich enough to impose a metric on their common domain, can be isometrically embedded within a compact perception pair. Similarly, it's proven that the space of non-expansive group invariant operators can be isometrically embedded into a compact space of the same, provided the operators' images form a cover over their codomain, resulting in new compact perception pairs that compactify their original counterparts, which possess totally bounded datasets.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this, researchers investigate whether this analogy accurately describes the collective behavior of quantum Hall states and other chiral topological systems. By analyzing the Haldane model, which simulates different environmental conditions, they examine the consequences of two scenarios: one with variable gravity and electrostatic forces, and another with variable temperature and chemical potential resulting from interactions with surrounding electrons and phonons. The study reveals that this analogy breaks down under certain conditions, specifically when interplay between quantum Hall states and the underlying lattice results in an intricate relationship between collective modes and the electronic charge. Consequently, the analogy's inaccuracy has significant implications for understanding the behavior of other chiral topological systems in the presence of underlying structures.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel technique outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  This paper investigates the effectiveness of using Transformer models to improve Automated Essay Grading.  To this end, we examine various data augmentation strategies to enhance the model's predictive accuracy.
