Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which characteristics of these prompts contribute to successful outcomes, thereby facilitating the development of more efficient prompt generation methods. We investigated the relationship between prompts and their performance in multi-choice tasks, and our analysis involved examining over 180,000 prompts across six datasets, as well as their corresponding evaluations. Our investigation sought to identify the predictive factors of prompt effectiveness, including common attributes associated with successful performance, and whether certain prompt types exhibit superiority.

We have computed the Benois $\mathscr{L}$-invariants for weight one cuspforms and their corresponding adjoint representations. Furthermore, our calculations extend Gross' $p$-adic regulator to non-critical Artin motives, which aligns with Deligne's framework. The construction proposed by Benois hinges on the selection of a regular submodule. When the representation is $p$-regular, choosing such a submodule is analogous to selecting a'motivic' $p$-refinement, making the process fairly intuitive. However, when the representation is $p$-irregular, things become more intricate as regular submodules are categorized by a flag variety, resulting in an endless selection of candidates. Despite these complications, our analysis in select examples highlights how Hida theory and eigencurve geometry can facilitate the identification of a well-defined'motivic' $p$-refinement.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve these challenges, we've 
successfully integrated Rydberg atoms with deep learning algorithms, allowing the 
model to leverage the atoms' sensitivity to electric fields while minimizing 
the impact of noise and interference. In a simulated experiment, the combined 
approach enabled accurate frequency recognition even when significantly 
overwhelmed by artificial noise and frequency interference.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a distinct disk structure, inferred from low surface brightness (LSB) galaxies. Using photometric and kinematic analysis, we investigate the galactic disk of UGC 8839 to determine the causes of the prominent HII region. Photoelectric radial surface brightness profiles demonstrate that the galaxy has a very extended disk, comparable to those of other LSB galaxies. However, its central disk is noticeably thicker than its counterparts in the studied sample. A comprehensive investigation through various templates including optical and radioband spectra, reveals that the HII region in UGC 8839 is situated at the edge of its thin outer disk, similar to the case with the other galaxies. Despite some exceptional features, UGC 8839 exhibits a generally stable thick disk, consistent with those of other galaxies in the sample. Interestingly, the HII region in UGC 8839 exhibits similar characteristics to a known star-forming region in another galaxy, the near-by spiral NGC 4414, suggesting two possible scenarios to explain its formation - one involves the interaction with a galactic halo companion or a passing dwarf galaxy, or it received a burst of gas from a major galactic merger in the recent past.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range of 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under a specific growth constraint.

Using the Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer on board the Mars Atmospheric and Volatile Evolution/NASA Mars Science Laboratory mission, the oscillating CO$_{2}$ density in the upper Martian atmosphere, spanning between 120 and 190~km in altitude, is monitored. This observation sheds light on the effects of gravity waves (GWs), allowing scientists to analyze the behavior of GWs in the upper atmosphere under isothermal conditions and understand the role that the atmospheric background temperature plays in the propagation of GWs. Data obtained from past missions including the Mars Global Surveyor, the Mars Odyssey, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, in combination with the new MAVEN findings, reveal an association between GW-induced density disturbances and the atmospheric background temperature, primarily found in the ODY mission's data collected over polar regions, rather than in the MGS and MRO datasets. Conversely, MRO's observations of the upper Martian atmosphere's behavior exhibit an association between GW-induced density disturbances and the Brunt-V\"{a}is\"{a}l\"{a} frequency. It is found that, in the atmospheric layer extending between 100 and 120~km in altitude, GW-induced density disturbances no longer correlate with temperature, instead aligning with atmospheric stability, whereas, in the three datasets collected by MGS, MRO, and ODY at non-polar latitudes, the intensity of the observed gravity waves does not correlate with temperature stability, instead pointing towards the role that the source

The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an electromagnetic field, acting as a source of photons, which can then interact either with other photons or with hadrons. Specifically, ultra-peripheral collisions occur when high-energy ions surpass the range of the strong force, facilitated by virtual photons exchanged between the nuclei, whose numbers directly correlate with the nuclear charge. Given its exceptional energy levels, the LHC serves as the most powerful photon source ever constructed, particularly in favouring photoproduction of heavy vector mesons due to their inherent affinity to photons. Recent experiments examining the forward J/psi production in lead-lead ultra-peripheral collisions at 5.02 TeV using the ALICE detector are featured.

Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation involve selecting short, low-quality sounds and using sampling-based methods. However, current models using top-notch graphics processing units can still take several minutes to process a single frame. Our approach presents a unified model able to process visually guided sound generation quickly, using information up to 16 frames in advance, and producing higher quality sounds. Our system able to quickly identify the most suitable sound and essential modifications needed. For the most challenging conditions, pre-trained models can achieve comparable results to state-of-the-art methods, while also producing longer sound sequences. Our model's efficiency allows it to process sounds up to 16 frames in advance, and in test scenarios under real-time constraints, it consistently outperforms the leading method. Our work represents a significant step towards using visual guidance to generate high-quality sounds in a rapid and efficient manner.

Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, leveraging their capacity to incorporate temporal context and make sequential predictions. In recent years, they've seen widespread adoption across various tasks, including language modeling, sentence translation, image description, text classification, and stock market forecasting. Our aim is to introduce the fundamental concepts of recurrent neural networks, highlighting their applications in sequential tasks and the multiple variants available, such as LSTM and GRU.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, and attributes this finding to the broader concept of 'economic irreversibility,' illustrating its analogy to the principles of thermodynamics. A fundamental inequality provides a framework for the implementation of such measures. A novel theoretical approach underlying this methodology contributes to the body of econophysics research.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation set accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings.

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices.

This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Experiments have demonstrated that at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa, the material's anomalous Hall effect is completely eliminated. The pressure-dependent magnetization study revealed that as pressure increased, Mn$_3$Sn shifted from a conventional antiferromagnetic ground state to a helical state, where the anomalous Hall effect is suppressed. The key factor behind this phenomenon is the length difference between the adjacent atoms in Mn$_3$Sn, where a 1% increase leads to a complete disappearance of the anomalous Hall effect. The entire pressure-dependent phase diagram of Mn$_3$Sn was measured, showing that the transition from the antiferromagnetic to the helical state occurs between 1.5 and 2.5 GPa, with the appearance of a mysterious Hall effect state at intermediate pressure levels. Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect of it. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital knowledge automatically from natural language texts. By automatically
identifying semantic relationships between entities, RE contributes significantly to the
domain. This synopsis highlights recent developments in RE, specifically focusing on the
emergence of deep neural network-based approaches, their underlying challenges, and the
subsequent advancements in RE evaluation methods.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by 312% in multiple test sets.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data and
describe the inner body structures. Preparing these reports necessitates medical
experts to be familiar with both normal anatomy and the detection of anomalies.
Current medical image analysis systems lack the knowledge of anatomical structure
appearance due to difficulty in collecting annotated data, thus restricting their
capability to narrow expertise areas, like diagnosing specific conditions. Our
research addresses this gap by incorporating human anatomy and allowing the
connection between report content and corresponding image content. To utilize
anatomical information, we introduce an advanced system to gather and integrate
human body structures from CT scans and incorporate it into PAXRay. The latter is
a comprehensive dataset for X-Ray anatomical structure segmentation. Our results
show that employing anatomical information significantly enhances visually linking
radiologists' observations with images, as our segmentations result in a 50%
better grounding outcome on the OpenI dataset compared to commonly used region
proposal methods. The PAXRay dataset is accessible at https://constantinseibold.
github.io/paxray/.

Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a limited range and then made an educated guess that this range is the absolute minimum. Subsequent work by a different researcher, collaborating with David Gabai, found counterexamples that contradict this theory. Due to the connection between tight contact structures and taut foliations, researchers now consider the possibility that this theory could hold for tight contact structures, which are also related to Euler classes of one. To test this idea, recent findings show that previously found counterexamples are also related to tight contact structures, leaving room for the possibility that this theory might be correct for tight contact structures.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its applicability is limited to simple cases. Consequently, we put forth a new criterion based on the angular semivariance, offering a versatile method for assessing emission directionality that is both model-independent and applicable in multiple situations.

Our analysis focuses on the stability of cryptocurrency prices in relation to their
use as a medium of exchange. The study takes an unconventional approach by
concentrating on price consistency rather than investigating the underlying
influence of economic principles. The research introduces a stability metric, BIS,
to gauge the predictability of cryptocurrency price movements. The findings reveal
that most cryptocurrencies exhibit unpredictable price behavior, with only a few
exhibiting stable trends. The research further identifies that stable prices are
more likely to be found in cryptocurrencies with higher trading volumes and those
that have been active for a longer period.

By integrating analytical methods including field theory, probability and integrability, we resolve the large deviation issue of the KPZ equation at early time periods. Expanding the existing weak noise theory, which reformulates large deviations into a nonlinear hydrodynamics problem, we reveal its complete solvability through a link with the integrability of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Employing the inverse scattering technique and a newly developed Fredholm determinant framework, we arrive at exact solutions that depend on specific initial conditions and reveal a myriad of intricate behaviors.

The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed with data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. Utilizing both the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and calibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the Spin Plane Double Probe, researchers are able to investigate turbulent patterns down to specific frequencies. These measurements are then applied to various solar wind plasma intervals. One such interval is scrutinized, yielding valuable insights into its power spectral density fluctuations spanning from the inertial to sub-ion range. Two possible explanations for these density patterns exist, suggesting that they are a result either of specific wave types and interactions at varying scales or a broader physical phenomenon, the Hall effect. These theories are substantiated through the examination of associated electric field data.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2-10 nm wavelength, yielding high peak powers of hundreds of megawatts, with a potential for delivering over a thousand pulses per second to enable groundbreaking attosecond science applications.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is developed, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order partial differential equation is formulated, similar to the Laplace equation, yet with a different boundary condition. However, this difference results in no approximate solution being available compared to the Laplace equation, except in extremely rare instances. To address this, a physical optics approach is applied, drawing from work by Kirchhoff and others, to provide a practical solution for determining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and
allowed for the identification of biased districting plans.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the proposed technique applies low-rank decomposition to differentiate the background from defect information within the fabric's image blocks. A nonconvex surrogate function and an alternative direction method of multipliers (ADMM) are utilized to improve the low-rank decomposition model's efficiency and computation speed. Ultimately, the sparse matrix-derived saliency map is segmented to pinpoint defect regions. Experimental findings demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques and successfully detects fabric defects.

To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment. Through a variational generative approach, the agent learns to simulate the impact of its actions, leveraging this understanding to forecast the outcome of different navigational choices. As a result, the agent achieves improved cross-target and cross-scene generalization capabilities, outperforming current state-of-the-art models by at least 10% according to AI2-THOR evaluations. Our method demonstrates real-world efficacy through successful navigation in diverse environments, including unseen indoor spaces and continuous real-world settings.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast to the radii of Schwarzschild black holes, the Bonchi mass aspect does not provide a suitable measure of the particles and antiparticles scenario.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a population synthesis model, assuming the binary systems initially formed in the gas disk surrounding the primordial fragment. Our analysis takes into account the effects of population III binary reionization and a variable population III binary merger rate due to three-body interactions with a massive black hole. We find that about 30 percent of population III binary remnants can survive and reside within nuclear star clusters. Our study also focuses on the gravitational waves emitted from population III binary remnants in nuclear star clusters, considering both detectable and undetectable signals by LISA. For the most realistic scenario, our population III binary remnants in nuclear star clusters can be detected by LISA up to 100 pc from the massive black hole's center with a detection rate of around one event in every two years at this distance. Our research shows that LISA can potentially detect up to six events from this source in the first year of operation.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on active and reactive power control strategies for ESS.

Our study focuses on how the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons contribute to the radiative decays $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$. The first process is predominantly driven by the $\omega$ meson. On the other hand, the cascade decays involving the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons are substantially suppressed compared to other diagrams, specifically those that go through the $\psi(2S)$ or a three-body decay of $\rho$. The measured branching ratios for $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ are potentially within reach for the BESIII and LHCb Collaborations. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi\pi^+\pi^- \gamma$ decays may be used to establish the X(3872) nature and study its constituents.

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

Text-based games provide a versatile platform to explore AI, with numerous applications in virtual assistants, search, and content recommendation. As challenges in text-based games progress, current technologies often fall short, failing to adapt to changing situations and requiring significant reinforcement learning data to make progress. Our text-based game engine, TextWorldExpress, is an optimized tool for developing complex games that can be up to 100 times more efficient than other engines, thanks to its innovative use of techniques such as caching, pre-computed responses, and artificial language generation to reduce the number of possible states and actions. This optimized engine enabled it to achieve a remarkable million steps per second, marking a notable advancement in the field. Our study involved conducting a comprehensive comparison of various AI techniques, including rule-based systems and reinforcement learning using deep neural networks, in four intricate games created with TextWorldExpress, revealing substantial performance enhancements and offering valuable insights for future research.

The study on varying electron spin orientation employs the coordinate transformation method. Characteristically, Topological Insulators exhibit an uneven spin orientation shift within the Brillouin zone. In cases of defects, this shift occurs along closed paths in the sample's contour and is measured by the spin hall conductivity, expressed as the integral of the electron spin's cross product with its velocity along this contour. This formulation simplifies the determination of spin orientation shifts in modified topological insulators, defective topological insulators, and topological varients. Additionally, it demonstrates that the spin orientation shift in the thomson hole of the Dirac equation and modified topological insulators can be resolved geometrically.

For the case when $p > 1$, we will demonstrate that if $\phi_1 > 0$ and $(\vec{\phi},r) \in C^1 \left( (0,\pi), \mathbb{R}^2 \right)$ satisfies the equation $\Delta_r \vec{\phi} = 0$, then $\phi_2 \leq 0$ in the sector $\{ (r \cos \theta, r \sin \theta) : r \in (0,\pi), \theta \in (0,\phi_1(r)) \}$. Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers.

Ravindra's conjecture, regarding the finiteness of non-isomorphic polynomial maps over a number field to another, has been a prominent issue in rational chaos theory. Although Milne introduced a related theorem to provide bounds, the theorem's utility is limited due to the complexity of identifying the essential part of the Galois action. Notably, the work of Rousseleroche introduced new tools and proved the conjecture under a specific condition for highly degenerate maps. Additionally, the author's prior research introduced a new approach to rational function maps in a different context. This paper combines those methods with the concept of'multi-sections' to extend the method of partial finiteness to include maps that are not necessarily polynomial, provided they have a specific level of degeneration.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data
and task-dependent information, significantly contributing to teaching robots human-like motion.
However, the approach faces the challenge of domain adaptation, as the approach is initially trained
using data from a single source and is then applied to a different domain with varying shapes and sizes.
In this research, a new method is introduced to tackle the domain adaptation problem by transporting
the trained manipulability ellipsoids to the new domain through a point-by-point comparison of corresponding features.
Furthermore, the approach sets up an optimization problem to align the source and target domains
by projecting them onto a manifold with a well-defined geometric structure, enabling efficient 3D point cloud alignment.
The method was thoroughly evaluated using a variety of objects with differing shapes and sizes.
The performance of the new approach was compared to existing methods and found to be more efficient and accurate.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine how to differentiate the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible top quark pair background. Specifically, we investigate the effectiveness of separating signals and backgrounds based on kinematic characteristics and cross-re références, focusing on final states with four b-jets and missing transverse momentum.

A novel method is introduced that learns the 3D pose of an object from a single view by observing the object rotate in an unstructured, real-world setting with little to no human intervention. Object poses with ambiguous identifications are tackled through robustness techniques, including pose symmetry and partial object views. This method is evaluated on a new dataset, 'Accidental Turntables', which consists of automatically detected turntables in unstructured environments with low-cost, unmanned systems. Additionally, the method's applicability is demonstrated in a 3D animation software that enables the creation of dynamically rotating 3D objects with accurate physical constraints.

Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework can discern one's attitude toward this misinformation. This new framework leverages neural networks and attitude consistency to classify stances toward COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. A novel neural framework, utilizing knowledge graphs to organize stances, successfully identifies attitudes toward this misinformation with outstanding results, outperforming other current best practices. Experiments were conducted on the recently created CoVaxLies dataset, a comprehensive collection of COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation gathered from Twitter discussions. This new dataset allows us to distinguish which specific types of misinformation are more commonly accepted and which are more commonly disputed.

Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential to unveil the core electronic behavior of matter, contingent on achieving two interconnected technological milestones linked to high-order harmonic generation sources. Firstly, achieving a higher photon flux would allow researchers to measure even the faintest electronic processes, while also attaining better spectral tunability would grant selectivity in targeting specific electronic transitions. Breakthroughs are made feasible by parametric waveform synthesis, giving scientists the capability to craft controllable, highly-tunable high-energy electric transients. Our findings demonstrate that by manipulating the waveform of the driving laser pulse via its relative phase and carrier-envelope phase, it's possible to exert fine-grained control over attosecond pulse characteristics. This innovation not only amplifies experimental possibilities in the realm of attosecond science, but also paves the way for a highly sophisticated, electric-field-based manipulation of the electronic states within molecules.

Eclipse predictions for binary stars with three or more known components are significantly complicated by the presence of additional stars in the system. A new algorithm has been developed to forecast eclipses in such systems by accounting for the movement of third bodies, which has resulted in the identification of unobserved companion stars in several systems. The paper provides an overview of the new program and presents the results of his recent observations, which have confirmed that three systems contain an additional star orbiting around the primary pair. The newly discovered companion stars have been added to the database of multiple star systems, which now contains 116 systems and 137 companion stars.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that accounts for the boundary terms.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to computational efficiency are required for this approach. To address this need, enhancing training point generation is an important direction of investigation. Both adaptive and quasi-uniform sampling techniques have previously been explored, each showing benefits. To leverage these insights, we introduce Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation, which combines an adjustable nodal distribution method and a memory mechanism. We then conduct experiments on both linear and nonlinear PDEs, evaluating its accuracy and efficiency relative to traditional sampling methods.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by analyzing the oscillations in their electrostatic conduction band profile, which are characteristic of these devices. We model these dynamics by solving coupled two-dimensional Poisson's equations and energy equations, and find that the system converges to a stable thermodynamic state through energy minimization. Our analysis also shows that the movement of domain walls within the ferroelectric material leads to the negative capacitance effect, which in turn affects the device's drain current and variability due to the domain period. We also investigated how the domain wall's soft or hard state transition influences the device's electrical properties and transport. Our simulations are verified through both experimental data and phase-field modeling.

A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the Cargo ecosystem's architecture and how vulnerability dissemination occurs within it. Existing studies that generalize security management approaches across multiple ecosystems often overlook the unique technical characteristics of individual ecosystems, hindering direct applicability of security governance strategies to Cargo. To address this disparity, this research employs knowledge graph techniques to construct a dependency vulnerability graph for Cargo and presents an innovative algorithm that identifies vulnerability dissemination paths and degrees, as well as reveals Cargo ecosystem security-related metrics, including the central security component, most vulnerable module, widest vulnerability dissemination scope, and most vulnerable authorship groups. Our findings provide foundational insights into the Cargo ecosystem's security architecture and can be utilized for further research or even inform an automated security solution.

For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to demonstrate irreducibility. This paper confirms the irreducibility of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subjected to discrete jump noises and influenced by transport processes such as rotation and diffusion. The study also applies this irreducibility to establish ergodic behavior in systems like jump-affected rotator systems and a model of polymeric fluid dynamics that includes chain motion.

For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing the minimal vertex degree in its power graph. This power graph connects vertices based on one being a positive power of the other. By examining the group's prime divisors and Sylow subgroups, we've pinpointed vertices related to its cyclic subgroups. This allows us to establish a connection between the group's properties and its minimal vertex degree in the power graph. This study provides degree calculations for specific types of noncyclic abelian groups.

Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been extensively studied at high-energy ranges above sqrt(s) = 63 GeV using the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings. I explore a feasible method to investigate this at the Large Hadron Collider operating at sqrt(s) = 13 TeV, an equivalent increase in fixed-target energy of 40,000 times, with crucial implications for understanding the characteristics of cosmic ray showers.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, utilizing a matrix factorization framework with a sparsity prior to reduce overparameterization. Through the propagation of this sparsity, our OCNs can operate with a reduced number of parameters compared to standard DCNNs. Our experimental results show that OCNs achieve superior performance on datasets subject to orientation transformations, with a particular advantage over state-of-the-art methods on the CIFAR-10A dataset.

This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's geometric structure is efficiently propagated across the GCN through KNN search. This insight drives the simplification of multiple KNN searches in GCNs, allowing us to replace them with a single search that equally well captures the point cloud's global structural features. Additionally, we find that the permutation infulness of GCNs enables us to reduce the buffer size for matrix operations, thereby reducing memory consumption and data redundancy within the network. We validate the efficiency of our optimized GCN across three benchmark datasets, resulting in a notable speedup and reduced parameter count compared to the original method.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning but can take various forms visually. Unlike existing Trojan attacks, which embed inconsequential triggers in clean images, our method considers trigger images as full-resolution representations of meaningful object classes. As our backdoored classifier is designed to recognize the inherent concepts of trigger images rather than specific patterns, it can be triggered by semantically similar images with distinct appearances, rendering our attack more applicable and resilient to countermeasures in real-world scenarios. Our experiments show that even with limited Trojan patterns, our approach can adapt to new trigger images within the same category and evade sophisticated defense strategies effectively.

We are developing an image slicer for the Magellan IMACS spectrograph to transform it into a spatially integrated device. The new system, called ROSIE (Magellan Optical Spectrograph for Integrated Experiments), will comprise 10 equally spaced 5x5 slicers, merging 50 individual spectra into 1, utilizing a 0.6" x 0.6" spatial resolution and 2.57 Angstrom/pix spectral resolution. The slicers will enable the ejection of up to 6 orders of the spectrograph into an echellette configuration, facilitating spatially resolved observations of up to 100 objects across 20 x 6 spatial slices. The projected cost of the modification is approximately $170,000, anticipated to enhance Magellan's capabilities in areas like absorption line spectroscopy, star formation research, and redshift hunting by expanding its observational scope to encompass spatially resolved tasks.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck {\it et al.} (Eur. Phys. J. A {\bf 56}, 97 (2020)) are considered to outline the pathway for enhancing low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor determinations via new Threshold Hand Mirror (THM) measurements.

A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets resembling Earth. New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition to predict the bulk composition and internal structures of these planets. In this research, we apply this concept to a sample of 13 stars that host terrestrial planets similar to our Sun, utilising high-precision data on their elemental composition. Based on this and other constraints, we simulated the detailed mineral makeup and internal structures of hypothetical habitable-zone exoplanets around these stars. Our model indicates that most of these planets are expected to have compositions and internal structures analogous to those of Earth. However, our analysis reveals two exceptions, the Kepler-10 and Kepler-37 planets, which would likely develop cores significantly smaller than Earth due to oxidation. Furthermore, our exploration of this unique stellar sample enhances the understanding of planetary building blocks and their variability.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. This leads to the conclusion that leveraging CSI directly may not be the most effective approach. On the other hand, extracting features from raw CSI via a DNN can mask the impact of system disturbances to some extent. To build upon this concept, this study proposes an innovative method that extracts features from the attention weights of CSI, rather than the CSI itself. The proposed method employs a multi-head attention mechanism to distill essential features from the input CSI. The experimental results indicate that the proposed method yields more accurate localization outcomes compared to conventional methods.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors.

We investigate functions defined on the vertices of the Hamming graphs H(n,q), focusing specifically on those with support contained in the direct sum of the eigenspaces U_i(n,q), U_{i+1}(n,q),..., U_j(n,q) where 0 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n. Under certain conditions, specifically when n is greater than or equal to the sum of i and j, and when the size of the alphabet is 3 or greater, we identify the functions with minimum possible support and establish a characterization for those with such a minimum. In scenarios where n is less than the sum of i and j, but with a sufficiently large alphabet size of at least 4, we identify similar properties of functions. In particular, we establish a characterization for the functions within the eigenspace U_i(n,q) with minimum possible support in several specific scenarios.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based interface that enables users to interact with COPASI models within their web browsers. We based ShinyCOPASI on the COPASI source code and incorporated it into a Ruby on Rails framework, utilizing Ruby on Rails to create a standalone web application. This new version allows for running all COPASI tasks, as well as uploading CSV files and performing tasks on multiple model species with similar initial and final conditions. Users can access ShinyCOPASI at https://shiny.copasi.org/ and learn its functionality at https://shiny.copasi.org/help/.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, diverse solution approaches, performance metrics, and improvement techniques is introduced. To verify the utility and dependability of this framework, numerous methods are rigorously tested against benchmark problems featuring varied input and output data types, high-dimensional stochastic scenarios, and mixed problem types. Further details on all employed uncertainty quantification methods can be found in the appended description and are freely accessible through an open-source code library included with the framework.

We are investigating quantum group analogues of the free group factors' radial subalgebras, specifically those of class functions, within the context of compact quantum groups. We found that the algebras of class functions for the free orthogonal quantum groups cannot be maximally abundant *-subalgebras (MASAs) under certain conditions. Central to our research is the concept of a quasi-split inclusion. We demonstrated that the inclusion of the class functions' algebra is quasi-split in certain unitary quantum group scenarios. Additionally, we showed that the resulting subalgebra is non-abelian. We obtained another key finding related to its relative commutant in such instances. In contrast, we constructed specific bicrossed products based on $SU_q(2)$ for which the class functions' algebra constitutes a MASA.

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of algorithms for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees, was introduced. This method is further exemplified through inexact GMRES policy iteration, which applies GMRES for the policy evaluation process. Notably, inexact GMRES policy iteration outperforms policy iteration and optimistic policy iteration by 5.8 and 2.2 times, respectively, in a 10000-state MDP.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this paper that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior.

This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate realistic data for Athens, Georgia, USA. To efficiently handle the large datasets produced by such simulators, an approach involves first selecting key points to approximate the output, and then applying a specialized method to estimate optimal input parameters at those points, while accounting for any uncertainty in the solution. A comprehensive simulation-based study compares the proposed technique with other established methods on a range of synthetic and real-world scenarios.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a robust model's accuracy and considering the influence of random example exposure, according to Gourdeau et al. (2019). Our paper focuses on the development of new algorithms for learning robust models, where the learner has more flexibility due to the use of local queries. We create the first distribution-free algorithms for achieving robust empirical risk minimization (ERM), a robust measure of model accuracy. Our first learning model utilizes local membership queries (LMQs), where the learner can verify the labels of nearby points to the training sample. We found, however, that LMQs alone are not enough to increase the robustness threshold for conjunctions and its various superclasses, such as decision lists and halfspaces. To address this issue, we developed a new local equivalence query (LEQ) oracle, which allows the learner to confirm whether a model's hypothesis and the target concept agree within a certain range, in addition to providing any existing counterexamples. We established a crucial separation result: while we found that robust learning is generally impossible for many concepts if the learner's query radius is significantly smaller than the adversary's allowed perturbation budget, our research also identified the conditions under which we can successfully develop robust ERM algorithms. We subsequently calculated the number of local queries required to execute these algorithms using the principles of online learning. Additionally, we further optimized the number of required queries for conjunctions.

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with a minimum transverse momentum of 1 GeV were tracked within a narrow cone around the jet axis. By comparing the fragmentation functions for jets in proton-proton and lead-lead collisions, variations in internal structure were identified. The fragmentation functions for jets in lead-lead collisions, above a certain number of colliding particles, reveal a lower yield of high-transverse-momentum particles and a shift towards lower-transverse-momentum particles.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an alternative approach. This involves the substitution of hyperbolic trigonometric 1-forms for their standard trigonometric counterparts.

Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously reported by Meisner et al in 2020, has yielded an assortment of peculiar attributes for the object. New images taken by Keck/MOSFIRE and HST/WFC3 cameras have established that the object is among a select few with extremely faint proper motion, indicating it has a very low temperature consistent with the coolest Y dwarfs. Moreover, the object possesses color indices of W1-W2 and ch1-ch2 about 1.6 mag bluer than a typical Y dwarf. New data collected from WISE, Spitzer, and HST for parallax measurement have determined a close distance of $16.3^{+1.4}_{-1.2}$ parsecs and a substantial transverse velocity of $207.4{\pm}15.9$ km/s. The calculated J, W2, and ch2 absolute magnitudes align with the coolest Y dwarfs despite W1-W2 and ch1-ch2 indices displaying a distinct discrepancy. Research suggests that the object is most likely an ancient metal-poor brown dwarf and possibly the initial instance of a Y subdwarf, necessitating further examination through broad-band spectroscopy and photometry using the JWST for validation of the hypothesis.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations of low 
proton-to-pion ratios relative to thermal models and rising $\phi$-to-pion ratios
with increased final-state particle count.

We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for NNLO DGLAP kernels and flavor matching.

Specimens made of Martian and Lunar soil substitutes, in the form of cylinders, were created using a combination of saltwater and heat, and then fired at various temperatures to analyze their internal structure, strength and contraction. The internal structures of these materials were studied under a microscope and their mechanical properties were tested using a universal testing machine. The experiment was performed twice using different types of simulants for Martian and Lunar soil, resulting in manufactured samples resembling traditional building blocks and the initial stages of 3D printing with a binder. The results indicated that the optimal firing temperature for both types of simulants lies between 1100 C and 1200 C. The compressive strength of these materials met the requirements for building structures on other planets, suggesting their potential for use as building materials in extraterrestrial construction and as a base material for additive manufacturing processes similar to 3D printing with a binder.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. The accuracy of the theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations and an underlying analysis shows that slip significantly increases the instability rate.

By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are generally accurate within expected margins of error for a set of 21 galaxies. Notably, even after accounting for uncertainties, the predictions do not show significant bias. To further verify the reliability of the model, we find that adjusting the model's parameters to match this observed data does not yield substantial changes.

This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a substantial number of the type II quantum subgroups within the specified categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. In this particular study, we classify the braided auto-equivalences of the local modules in categories linked to known type I quantum subgroups of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. It has been determined that the symmetries exhibited in this research are all non-exceptional, with the exception of the 'D-type' symmetry, which is an instance of a braided auto-equivalence of order four. Furthermore, we have developed relationships between the symmetries of the local modules and the central charges of the type I quantum subgroups, which will be explored in more detail within the accompanying paper.

The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome that contradicts conventional travelling wave approximations commonly utilised in the field.

This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to classify handwritten mathematical terms based on time series data from the DigiPen. The challenge involves recognizing mathematical expressions from 15 possible characters written by multiple individuals. To overcome the initial challenge, a data-driven and rule-based information extraction technique is applied to break down the labeled data. Following this process, two machine learning models are developed - the first is a binary classifier leveraging a hybrid Deep Neural Network and Random Forest to detect writing activities, and the second is a Deep Neural Network integrating convolutional and recurrent layers for single-character classification. Although the proposed approach demonstrates satisfactory accuracy and performance in the challenge evaluation simulation with an average Levensthein Distance of 8, its overall efficiency and real-time capabilities still require improvement.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech.

Species distribution analysis can be effectively conducted through occupancy modeling, taking into consideration inaccuracies in species detection data. To address multiple species, states, and data types, a unified approach called the state-space occupancy model has been developed. A recently created R package called spOccupancy for Visualizing Extinct Species aims to make this model easily applicable to single, multiple, and combined species, as well as incorporate spatial correlations. The package provides comprehensive functionality for model estimation and interpretation, including the ability to split states, integrate data from immatures and adults, utilize random forests, and compute and display predicted probabilities, mean occupancy rates, and expected densities. The package's spOccupancy3 function allows for the efficient computation of integrated occupancy models, including those with spatial correlations and multiple species, through the use of the Stan sampling algorithm. The package also includes various functions to handle model estimation with large data sets, moderate data sets, and simulated data, as well as a spOccupancy3Sim function to facilitate efficient computation of simulated data for model evaluation and confirmation.

This project's goal is to create an interactive AI system that aids dermatologists in identifying skin cancer by comparing query images with a wide range of skin lesion images, and showing the results in a ranked list with the query image. A comprehensive dataset of images, specifically tailored for this project, was created using a combination of publicly available data and custom images, totaling 250,000 entries. After conducting thorough experiments and evaluations, our team refined the design of the system and implemented a training schedule, resulting in a highly efficient model. With a well-planned training process, the system achieved exceptional accuracy, scoring over 90% in identifying malignant skin lesions on images, and demonstrated significant improvements over the current state-of-the-art techniques.

To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a probabilistic autoencoder that incorporates a Normalizing Flow component after initial training using an Auto-Encoder. The model's two-stage generative architecture can identify a reduced-dimensional representation of SNe Ia, accurately modeling their spectral evolution across wavelength and time directly from data. Introducing a penalty term to address variability correlations and a multi-stage training framework within our physically-parameterized network enabled the separation of intrinsic and extrinsic variability, eliminating the need for magnitude standardization models. The PAE was applied in several tasks to improve cosmological analyses, such as automatically detecting outliers, generating sample spectra consistent with data distribution, and resolving noisy inverse problems to estimate cosmological distances. Notably, we found three intrinsic model parameters yielded the best results, in line with existing research. The PAE achieved an optimal standardization of $0.091 \pm 0.010$ mag for our test sample of SNe Ia, reducing to $0.074 \pm 0.010$ mag when peculiar velocity contributions are removed. The project's code and pre-trained models are publicly available at \href{https://github.com/georgestein/suPAErnova}{github.com/georgestein/suPAErnova}.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been observed in a gravitationally lensed star-forming galaxy, which provides an expanded view of the outflow mechanism in young galaxies forming stars. The outflow was identified through data collected using the VLA radio telescope, with the outflow's properties being deduced by accounting for the galaxy's shape and the effects of gravitational lensing. The outflow's mass was estimated to be approximately 6.7$\times$10$^{9}$ M$\odot$, with an average velocity of around 402 km/s and a kinematically extended out to 20 kpc. Further analysis of the outflow was compared to hydrodynamic simulations, which has implied that the outflow is predominantly driven by radiation pressure, suggesting the need for observational constraints on the formation of galaxies via supermassive stars and top-level tails.

To study the movement of fluid into a swirling, turbulent plume containing heavy particles that sink more slowly than the plume moves, researchers used controlled experiments in a lab setting. The experiments focused on the parameters that influence the flow and the behavior of these sinking particles. The results revealed that the rate at which fluid enters the plume increases in direct proportion to the square of the difference between the flow rates below and above the plume, regardless of the density of the particles. The rate at which particles become entrained in the plume increases in direct proportion to the difference between the flow rates below and above the plume, regardless of the density of the particles. The rate at which fluid enters the plume increases in direct proportion to the square of the difference between the flow rates below and above the plume, regardless of the density of the particles. The rate at which particles become entrained in the plume increases in direct proportion to the difference between the flow rates below and above the plume, regardless of the density of the particles. The rates at which fluid enter the plume and particles become entrained in the plume increase significantly when the parameters that typically influence these rates - the height of the plume and the size of the particles - change substantially. The observations from the experiments suggest that the rates at which fluid enter the plume and particles become entrained in the plume can be highly variable due to the high rates of turbulence in the surrounding environment. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By adopting hyperedges to model these interactions, researchers can create more comprehensive models, leading to the creation of a stochastic Susceptible-Infected-Removed model on contact graphs and complex networks, showcasing the potential for non-trivial infectious thresholds. This inspires the search for spectral thresholds – the behavior of the largest eigen-matrix elements – governing the model's dynamics. Through theoretical analysis, numerical simulations, and a detailed case study of an outbroken pandemic, evidence supports the notion that a threshold exists at which the disease spreads exponentially, characterized by the largest eigenvalue of the increased infection matrix and the second-largest eigenvalue of the spread matrix.

Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Through advanced theoretical calculations, researchers investigated the behavior of spin polarization within the prototype ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayer, which has an in-plane magnetization orientation. Their investigation reveals that this ferromagnetic bilayer displays a rich pattern of spin texture within its uppermost valence bands, which arises from two unique spin cants resulting from the interplay of ferromagnetic order with both chirality and electrical polarization. One type of cant is a result of layer stacking asymmetry and valence state polarization, resulting in equivalent canting patterns on both layers. Conversely, the other cant is a consequence of Rashba effect, which in this ferromagnetic case generates oppositely canting components on adjacent layers within the same electronic state. Additionally, researchers formulated a set of rules governing spin polarization behavior within magnetic crystals based on their magnetic symmetry properties. Lastly, they found that applying compressive strain could effectively control the shape of spin texture within ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayers by creating valence-band states with spins that can be aligned.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition to the late main sequence. Given that these stars' internal dynamics are governed by $\alpha$-effect dynamos and the magnetic breaking mechanism, it is crucial to model their rotational velocity more accurately, using advanced equations like the buzzbee equation, to ensure consistency with observations. To improve upon existing theories, we are introducing a novel treatment for the magnetic breaking effect, one that is rooted in traditional concepts. Our study also contors for the effects of differential rotation and the magnetic field's overall geometry on a star's overall rotation. Furthermore, we are exploring possible magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars, using both theoretical equations and computer simulations. To improve our understanding of these processes, we are introducing a novel concept, the mean-field criterion for magnetic cycles, which is rooted in the concept of helicity in the magnetic field. Our study reveals the potential for quasicycles and anti-cycles, as well as star's 'life in the slow lane'.

Deep multimodal learning using K-fan deep Boltzmann machines offers a novel approach to combine multiple input sources. This method can learn a common representation using contrastive divergence and is applied to classification, information retrieval, and other related tasks. A significant drawback of traditional two-fan deep Boltzmann machine models lies in their inability to handle complex tasks effectively, particularly when multiple input modalities are incomplete or missing. We present a K-fan deep model, featuring a K-branch architecture for handling multi-input, multi-output tasks efficiently. Each branch of the model can comprise multiple layers of neural networks. A shared representation is learned in a discriminative manner to tackle multiple tasks. We propose two optimization methods to ensure the entire model can be trained on a relatively small dataset efficiently. Moreover, we conduct experiments on multi-input, single-output tasks and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model through improved performance on datasets consisting of multiple modalities.

The use of model checking has become increasingly essential in validating the correctness of multi-threaded programs. Traditional unit and functional tests are insufficient due to the hidden nature of race conditions, which can evade detection by these tests. The McMini model checker, which is based on DPOR, has been expanded with a mechanism that enables the declaration of novel, fundamental thread operations through C code. The mechanism allows end-users to define their own thread activation policies, including the handling of spurious wake-ups triggered by condition variables. By specifying (i) when operations are allowed, (ii) which thread operations are mutually independent, and (iii) when operations can co-occur, users can define their own customized thread activation policies. Additionally, users can define custom wake-up policies by specifying when wait operations, such as those involving semaphores or condition variables, are permitted. A new enqueue thread operation was introduced, which allows users to define custom wake-up policies, such as first-in, first-out, last-in, first-out, and arbitrary order, and so forth. The McMini model checker's efficiency was validated through its correct and efficient operation in testing traditional multi-threaded constructs like mutexes, semaphores, and reader-writer operations. Furthermore, its extensibility was evaluated using novel, useful thread operation paradigms such as readers and two writers, demonstrating an up to fivefold speedup in model checking compared to traditional implementations using locks and condition variables.
