At the detrapping angle, key metrics such as survival probability and participation ratio exhibit one-parameter scaling behavior. Moreover, we demonstrate that the participation ratio grows with time, specifically in a logarithmic-corrected linear fashion, thereby resolving reported sublinear tendencies.

This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features "surface-level" characteristics similar to those of supervised convnets, but also possess "deeper" properties resulting from the model's inherent structure. These properties facilitate more efficient learning from limited data and allow ViT to achieve accurate results in low-data settings. To highlight the unique features of self-supervised ViT, we developed a data augmentation technique, called the spatial information loss, to emphasize the value of higher-position ViT tokens, and employed it in various downstream tasks, demonstrating its advantages over conventional convnets and self-supervised convolutional networks. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model has the capability to effectively explain the observed characteristics of the cosmic history.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), enabling the diffusion process to be directed by multiple, varying semantic axes, thereby permitting refined edits to images and changes in style, composition, and artistic vision. Furthermore, SEGA facilitates the exploration of latent spaces, providing insights into the complex concepts, like 'carbon emission,' learned by the model. We illustrate the Stable Artist's capabilities through multiple tasks, demonstrating its ability to create high-quality, tailored images and compositions.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised and supervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude.

High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, present throughout the solar cycle. These features, extensively detected in solar images, play a significant role in understanding the solar atmosphere's behavior, particularly in addressing the long-standing issue of coronal heating. This research aimed to examine the size, speed, and distribution patterns of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere, using datasets from the SOT/Hinode and HiFI/GREGOR telescopes, to gain insights into their characteristics. Employing an automated algorithm to detect magnetic bright points, their movements were tracked, and their statistical properties were analyzed, revealing distinct distributions of area, diameter, and speed. The results indicate that these characteristics exhibit two-component structures, pointing to the presence of two distinct populations of magnetic bright points, associated with different types of magnetic flux elements, and influenced by the varying spatial resolutions of the telescopes used.

Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike existing deep networks, humans exhibit more adept performance in these complex configurations, highlighting missing dynamic vision mechanisms in current models.

Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries and ordinary matter through kinetic mixing result in the manifestation of magnetic monopoles in our universe as microscopic, membrane-like entities. This interplay between micro-monopoles and cosmic strings in the early universe could have generated the galactic magnetic fields we observe today. However, the hypothetical monopoles act as highly efficient magnets, attracting protons from stars and interstellar gas, which would have led to a protons loss and a reduction in stellar lifetimes. This would have eventually caused a stellar death threshold within our Milky Way, occurring around 3-4 billion years ago. Since the galaxy's stellar death threshold failed to materialize, it is assumed that the magnetic fields in our galaxy are a result of its rotation rather than micro-monopoles. This theory is not in conflict with observations from stars within our galaxy. Additionally, the proposed monopoles are predicted to be concentrated mainly inside the Earth and are anticipated to be detected in experiments using high-energy beams to scan the Earth.

The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research area has immense potential to utilize AI in real-time weather forecasting. This work addresses the challenge of accurate weather prediction by leveraging the video transformer network, which enables it to effectively analyze time-series data sequences. Building on this foundation, we present an enhanced video transformer network, specifically the VIT4WE, by integrating CSWA into its encoder to securely aggregate and combine multi-scale spatial and temporal characteristics from the input data and effectively fuse them with each other, thus enhancing the video transformer's capability to extract more comprehensive spatial and temporal features, ultimately resulting in improved predictive performance, particularly an 8.6% increase in the accuracy of numerical weather forecasts over the existing video transformer network. Furthermore, we conducted exhaustive experiments to demonstrate that our proposed model consistently achieves superior predictive outcomes, surpassing state-of-the-art benchmark results, as well as provides meaningful visual insights that guide feature extraction and prediction by analyzing the attention weights of the video transformer and the CSWA module.

In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a basis can be found where the symmetry prevents coupling, leading to viable dark matter candidates. Specifically, we analyze the $S_3$-symmetric three-Higgs-doublet models that allow softly broken $S_3$ terms, determining which models can host dark matter. The variety of models arises from different arrangements of vacuum expectation values, leading to vacua with either one or two vanishing expectation values. In our research, we consider a scenario where the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, a remnant of $S_3$, stabilizes the dark matter candidate. Our study focuses on two models: one with CP violation and another without, each consisting of a single dark matter candidate and two active scalar sectors behaving similarly to a Type-I two-Higgs-doublet model. After investigating these models under various constraints, we identified potential masses for the dark matter candidate. In the case with CP violation, we found possible mass ranges of $[52.5, 89]~\text{GeV}$ or $[6.5, 44.5]~\text{GeV}$.

A comprehensive study on the PPT square conjecture is presented with a notable achievement: the PPT square conjecture's validity has been rigorously demonstrated for the case involving finite-dimensional space.

Intracellular transportation is crucial for delivering vital substances to complex branched neural structures, enabling their survival and operation. Disruption of this process is associated with various neurodegenerative diseases, making it vital to understand how neurons control transportation to target essential areas. We introduce a new optimization model that simulates the material transportation mechanism in complex neural geometries by minimizing congestion. The model adheres to partial differential equations that describe transportation based on molecular-motor-assisted models and is solved in complex tree structures through isogeometric analysis. We test our model by introducing different parameters that mimic traffic congestion and observe how alterations in factors such as microtubule density and motor protein number impact transportation efficiency. Our approach provides a framework for investigating the material transportation mechanism in neurons and can potentially be applied to target-based therapy development.

Billion-dollar losses inflicted by banking fraud across the globe make graph-based fraud detection in transactions increasingly significant. In analyzing transaction patterns, researchers utilize graphs to identify novel and complex schemes. This research aims to identify real-world transaction network patterns, specifically network motifs within a heterogenous transaction dataset. We also present a method for generating genuine banking transaction graphs via randomization. The outcome of our preliminary analysis indicates that extracting network motifs can reveal meaningful and understandable patterns within the data.

In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources. The energy emitted from the accretion process initially manifests as brief, high-frequency bursts at each close approach, but eventually, the surrounding disc becomes a sustained source of radiation, emitting a full spectrum of electromagnetic and gravitational waves.

Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions with light hadrons and CP symmetry violations, can provide insight into these processes. Studies of weak electromagnetic interactions rely on form factors to describe the hadronic part of the final states, which can be further understood by decomposing the hadronic current into specific orbital angular momentum components. Given the increasing data availability from future experiments, a new description of the hadronic currents is presented in terms of the quantum numbers of the final hadronic state using the isobar model. Additionally, the work includes formulas for orbital angular momenta and the rules for describing the decay chains of arbitrary mass hadronic three-body systems, which also improves existing descriptions in terms of form factors.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between $0$ and $1$ and $\beta$ is greater than $0$. The inverse of each $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ function, denoted as $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, represents a semimetric for all possible subsets of a given set. Our research found that the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is indeed a metric if $\alpha$ lies within the interval from $0$ to $0.5$ and $\beta$ is greater than or equal to $1/(1-\alpha)$. The verification of this outcome was successfully demonstrated in the Lean proof assistant. This parametrized space contains extreme points including $J_1 = D_{1/2,2}$, known as the Jaccard distance, and $J_{\infty} = D_{0,1}$, an analogue of the Li-Ma-Vit\'anyi information distance (2004) that has been normalized.

Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only before training, a constraint that becomes impractical with large datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an on-the-fly data augmentation technique to create blurry inputs dynamically during training and testing. To make the most of this approach, we adopt an unconventional framework incorporating a sequential process of blur removal and subsequent reblurring with the assistance of a module that mimics real-world blur, as well as hand-crafted prior information based on advanced statistical human body models. This module not only enhances the deblurring algorithm's ability to distinguish between human and non-human regions but also improves overall outcomes compared to other recent state-of-the-art methods through adversarial learning.

Hebb's theory suggests that synaptic connections adjust based on related brain activity patterns, leading to functional connection linkage and efficient data processing in complex neural systems. A hypothesis is proposed that living cells utilize chemical signal mechanisms to implement Hebb's principles through specialized electrical properties at synapses. Although the theory is significant in understanding brain functions, its practical application is limited in modern electronics due to its binary nature. However, this constraint can be overcome by utilizing multi-state digital technologies that emulate complex synaptic behaviors. Furthermore, by integrating these with custom electronic neurons, a digital system can be developed that replicates Hebb's theory and demonstrates intelligent connection formation and data processing within a digital framework.

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill the open completeness property in the refined version, whereas its original cardinality dictates whether the refined version is complete.

Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science increasingly rely on applying sophisticated AI models to comprehensive, discipline-specific datasets. However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a large dataset are excessively expensive, rendering them impractical to execute. As a result, existing benchmarking strategies are forced to compromise by utilizing small, select datasets, thereby risking both incomplete coverage of the data features and the omission of potentially significant model properties. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel dataset profiling approach that enables the efficient extraction and characterization of valuable information from extensive datasets at a reduced computational cost, enabling the identification of distinct features, groups, and patterns within the data. This characterized dataset can then be employed to develop an abstract representation of the data, allowing for the identification of suitable AI models to process and analyze the data effectively, thereby enriching the data with meaningful insights, thus enhancing the data quality and the accuracy of the resulting AI model predictions. We demonstrate the efficacy of our dataset profiling method using the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph with t vertices. This has been reinforced by another theory suggesting if a given graph is assigned t colors, where a certain set of its vertices uses every possible color, then that graph must have a complete graph with t vertices within it. This more robust idea has been tested with success for the case of t = 4. This result holds further implications if the underlying theory can be verified for 5 colored graphs, as it would necessarily validate the original Hadwiger's conjecture for 5 colored graphs, implying there could be a constant threshold value beyond which this original Hadwiger's conjecture is always in effect.

This research introduces an advanced algorithm for efficiently recovering smooth graph signals through generalized correntropy, and a specific loss function is formulated accordingly. Derived from the aforementioned principle, the algorithm is developed further, and a variant leveraging kernel width adaptation is presented. Results indicate that this adaptive kernel width variant surpasses the fixed kernel approach. In addition, the research undertakes theoretical examinations of the algorithm's properties. Firstly, the analysis focuses on proving the cost function's convexity. Secondly, the stability of the algorithm is analyzed under uniform conditions. Lastly, the mean convergence of the algorithm is assessed. Furthermore, the computational complexity of the algorithm is analyzed. Experiments conducted using synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the superiority of the proposed algorithm over existing methods for adaptive graph signal recovery.

Theoretical investigations are conducted to design and control entangled atomic states formed through spin-changing collisions within a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate for use in a more robust atom interferometry capable of withstanding common technical problems like detector limitations. It is discovered through both analytical and numerical examinations of the spin-changing collision process that utilizing a small initial disturbance as a trigger, as opposed to vacuum fluctuations, yields superior results despite reduced entanglement. Our findings have implications for optimizing entangled atomic state production for quantum-enhanced matter-wave interferometry applications.

The purpose of this research paper is to derive optimal estimates for the first eigenvalue of the first Robin eigenvalue problem involving the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator. This problem seeks to minimize a specific functional over all nonzero functions in the Sobolev space, and involves several variables and constants, including $p$, a bounded mean convex domain $\Omega$ in $N$-dimensional space, and a smooth norm $F$ on this space. We discovered new lower and upper bounds for this eigenvalue problem based on the first eigenvalue of a one-dimensional nonlinear problem. Specifically, for positive $\beta$ we proved a lower bound for the eigenvalue and for negative $\beta$ we proved an upper bound. Furthermore, for positive $\beta$ we were able to derive a lower bound for the eigenvalue in terms of the anisotropic inradius of the domain $\Omega$, and for negative $\beta$ we were able to derive an upper bound for the eigenvalue in terms of the parameter $\beta$.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process.

A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system that balances diversity and similarity. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple languages in diverse settings, and the results clearly indicate that our approach outperforms traditional self-training and state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning techniques by a significant margin.

We've investigated the transition form factors $f_+(q^2)$ and $f_-(q^2)$ [alternatively $f_0(q^2)$] for exclusive semileptonic $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ $(\ell=e,\mu,\tau)$ decays using the standard light-front quark model based on light-front quantization. Conventionally, $f_+(q^2)$ can be determined without considering troublesome elements, but $f_-(q^2)$ typically includes such difficulties. However, our study reveals in the Drell-Yan frame ($q^+=0$) that the results obtained using ${\cal F}_-(q^2)$ and $f_-(q^2)$ are comparable despite differing expressions and inclusions. Furthermore, in addition to calculating the form factors, we've provided transition probability values and compared our findings with experimental data and other theoretical model predictions.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (polynomial time) complexity, having demonstrated the capability to be contained within PTIME and yet unseparated from it. A prominent challenge lies in resolving the isomorphism problem for unordered Cai-Furer-Immerman graphs, known as the CFI-query, which has remained undefined within CPT despite being classified as a PTIME decision problem. A significant development has been achieved in understanding CPT's expressive power in addressing this issue by formulating a partial characterisation of solvable instances based on symmetric XOR-circuits for these specific graph types: In essence, for the CFI-query to be defined within a given graph class via CPT, each graph $G$ must allow for an equivalent XOR-circuit $C$, where $C$ can incorporate labelled edge inputs and satisfies specified circuit symmetry and property conditions. Furthermore, sufficient criteria for solvability within CPT have been established, along with a new algorithmic solution that uses a distinct input of structures containing suitable XOR-circuits. Building on earlier CPT-algorithms capable of addressing the CFI-query under specific input conditions (e.g., a predefined preorder and its associated colour classes of logarithmic size), our new findings implicitly extend this approach to accommodate preorders with colours of polylogarithmic size. These recent results for CPT, although theoretical in nature, hold the potential to become practically

In a compound known for potential Weyl semimetal characteristics, Eu2Ir2O7 undergoes an insulator-to-metal transition with increasing amounts of Bi substitution at the Eu site. To explore the properties of the resulting series, Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 was studied via HAXPES. Interestingly, Bi substitution unexpectedly led to a significant (20 %) reduction in the average spin magnetic moment of the Ir ions. The observed insulator-to-metal transition, accompanied by an increase in the Bi concentration, is associated with the emergence of a finite in-plane self-intermediate magnetic moment, which indicates the starting point of the material's potential Weyl semmetal formation.

Consider a metric space ${\mathfrak M}=({\mathcal M},\rho)$ and a set-valued mapping $F$ that maps ${\mathcal M}$ to the family ${\mathcal K}_m$ of all closed and compact subsets in ${\mathcal M}^m$. We define the core of $F$ as the set consisting of all elements $x\in{\mathcal M}$ for which there exists a mapping $f:F\to{\mathcal M}$ that is Lipschitz with parameter $\alpha=1$ and satisfies $f(F({\mathcal M}))={\mathcal M}$. We establish several essential properties, including that the core of $F$ is empty only if the diameter of the image is limited by $2\rho m$. This leads to the conclusion that if the diameter of $F({\mathcal M})$ is less than $2\rho m$, the core of $F$ includes the entire set ${\mathcal M}$. We also find that for a set of mappings $B$, the core of $F$ is contained in the set containing all selections of $F$ that are Lipschz with parameter $\alpha\leq1$. We develop several criteria to determine when a point belongs to the core of $F$ and establish relationships between these criteria for set-valued mappings that are Lipschz with parameter $\rho$. These results are further illustrated in specific

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting an arbitrary n-tuple at random as $P_n$ and investigate the resulting expression for the lower bound of $P_n$, $\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n$, as well as related problems involving the probability $P_{2n}$ that a particular double-sized n-tuple is both cyclic and nontransitive.

Many software systems have adjustable settings through run-time options, such as input parameters, allowing users to modify them to fulfill different purposes, such as reducing the system's footprint or improving security, yet these configurations often go unused in a specific system instance. In our research, we devised an experimental approach to reduce a system's configurable parameters during compilation and eliminate unnecessary settings on demand. A detailed analysis of the well-known video encoder x264 revealed the positive impact of such adjustments on the system's efficiency and security aspects, particularly in terms of binary size, exposure to security threats, and processing speed. Preliminary findings indicate that the systematic elimination of unused system options has a significant impact on the system's efficiency and security aspects, with the extent of these improvements tied to the number of removed options. Although our research underscores the importance of stripping unused system components, we still face the challenge of fully automating the system specialization process.

Light dark matter particles, particularly those weighing less than a GeV, offer an attractive option over heavier, weakly-interacting massive particles. Directly detecting such lightweight particles, however, poses a significant challenge. But if the recoil of a struck nucleus leads to electron ionization, it could potentially serve as a signal of dark matter interaction. Focusing on processes involving electron-electron and electron-nuclear interactions, researchers have simulated the effects of sub-GeV dark matter particles and established a method to differentiate such interactions from background noise. Using this approach, scientists can accurately pinpoint the range of parameters for dark matter cross-sections that match the observed background rates in current experiments. Specifically, researchers have found that the parameters for dark matter particles weighing between 1 and 10 MeV fall within the observed range of the SENSEI experiment's results. Researchers have further estimated the minimum reachable cross-sections that future experiments can achieve for both spin-dependent and spin-independent interactions. Specifically, researchers have found that the PPD experiment can set a new standard in this field, while future experiments can push this limit further.

This paper proposes a method to produce the most connected pairs of qubit states
via an anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction system, resulting in maximally entangled
anti-polariton qubits. The study further demonstrates how these entangled qubits
can be used for quantum teleportation, with the probability of successful transfer
being fully achieved after a specific time. Following the teleportation, the state
of the sender's qubit undergoes Rabi-like oscillations, while the receiver's qubit
remains in a mirror-image state.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy ECG signals is challenging due to interference from motion artifacts, baseline wander, and power line interference in remote health monitoring. Most existing research focuses on utilizing ECG lead selection to minimize noise's impact, but this also restricts signal availability and accessibility. This study proposes an innovative approach that utilizes all available leads to estimate IBIs, aiming to maximize signal quality and reliability. An RNN layer was implemented to model the ECG signal's temporal properties, followed by a Tiramisu-like RNN architecture for temporal feature extraction. The proposed method was compared with established techniques on the MIT-BIH arrhythmia database, showing superior performance in F-score terms: 0.923, 0.0. 0.886 for lead I, II, and III, respectively. Furthermore, this method's results demonstrate stochastic nature consistent with clinical expectations, outperforming other methods in terms of both accuracy and robustness.

We analyze large deviations of power input by an active force on an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) within or outside a confinement. Analytical calculations of the rate function are done for the free particle in any dimension using a saddle-point expansion. Additionally, a direct numerical approach via solution of the AOUP equations is performed, alongside a method using Legendre-Fenchel transform of the scaled cumulant generating function obtained via a cloning algorithm. Results for the free particle exhibit asymptotically linear behavior with a rate function that depends on specific force characteristics, while confinement scenarios exhibit distinct behavior based on particle motion patterns and an active force that acts either consistently or oppositely to thermal force.

This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations across a range of subjects. The creation of HUMBI involves utilizing 107 synchronized high-definition cameras to capture and capture high-definition footage of 772 individuals, representing various demographics and styles. Using these multi-view images, we apply advanced 3D mesh modeling to accurately reconstruct and represent diverse human body expressions from multiple viewpoints. The proposed dataset demonstrates exceptional efficiency in learning and reconstructing a complete human model, effectively supplementing existing human body expression datasets such as MPII-Gaze, Multi-PIE, Human3.6M, and Panoptic Studio datasets, which were previously limited to single viewpoints or fewer subjects. Based on HUMBI's capabilities, we outline a new benchmark challenge focused on leveraging pose data to generate highly realistic, three-dimensional human body expressions in the context of photorealistic reconstruction. The HUMBI dataset is accessible at http://humbi-data.net.

Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating English models to other languages can be costly and inefficient in the age of large datasets and advanced neural models. We propose a universal approach to seamlessly move neural models across languages by utilizing task definitions and embeddings, allowing for direct and efficient translation to other languages. We implement and test this method with neural machine translation and sentiment analysis models, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency in multiple languages including Spanish, French, and Chinese. Importantly, this method requires minimal changes to the original model and can be applied to any neural model and language without further modifications.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in the NTIRE 2021 challenge.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios.

We have improved the performance of heat engines working within specific timeframes, employing a time-varying energy function in conjunction with experimentally grounded limitations on the bath temperature and the ratio of temperatures. To achieve this, we have reduced the system's temperature differences, resulting in reduced entropy production, utilizing a thermodynamic efficiency metric that accounts for operational constraints. This novel approach is represented by a set of geometric, nonlinear, and dynamic limitations, influencing the system's trajectory in a heat transfer process. Furthermore, we have analytically established the maximum achievable efficiency for heat engines operating within specific timeframes, also known as thermodynamic Carnot efficiency. Moreover, we have found that our optimal heat engine protocol demonstrates self-averaging properties, especially in its thermal fluctuations. This finding confirms that the average behavior of the optimal protocol replicates the dynamics of its classical, smooth counterpart, despite significant thermal fluctuations in individual realizations.

This research proposes a probabilistic model that analyzes the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and these outcomes are presented as probabilistic contingency tables. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, the proposed model is applied to the simulation of 1000 random hurricane scenarios and compared with traditional power flow methods, utilizing data from the 2008 Southeastern US hurricane outbreak.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, and this correspondence serves as the foundation for an in-depth analysis of their invariant measures. Through initial investigation, we confirm the existence of two distinct ergodic measures with maximal entropy for these generalized baker maps, and also reveal the underlying cause for the failure of certain entropy-based approaches.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex model featuring additional particles. A critical method for resolving this query involves scrutinizing extended scalar models using future high-energy collider facilities, including the potential proton-proton collider with 27 and 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, and advanced lepton colliders at various energy levels.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals like piano and NSynth music. Experimental results show the effectiveness of QPNet in terms of generated signal quality, with the quality increasing by around 6 dB in terms of signal signal-to-noise ratio compared to WN with an equivalent number of parameters.

Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have become an integral part of our daily lives as consumers. However, their limitations become apparent when dealing with recommendation data due to the complexities and idiosyncrasies of user preferences. To overcome these challenges, researchers have integrated CF with Biclustering techniques to leverage data insights and improve system accuracy. This research builds upon existing work by developing an innovative Biclustering-based CF approach, employing an unsupervised Biclustering algorithm to discover unique patterns in recommendation data and subsequently create individualized user models. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through systematic experiments which reveal a notable enhancement in recommendation quality across various evaluation metrics.

Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found patterns distinct from a quiet star's spectrum by comparing active to quiet periods. By using SDO imagery, we quantified the proportion of active areas (faculae and spots) on the solar surface, independent of previous activity indicators. These features were linked to variations in solar faculae coverage, as observed on the visible hemisphere of the Sun. Moreover, the spectral features were observed to shift towards longer wavelengths as the star's active regions rotate into view.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in shape and location, its height may be affected by the resistance; however, it retains its characteristic behavior under varying resistance levels. In contrast, peaks from other sources show a variety of changes based on resistance levels: some may disappear, and others may split into multiple peaks. We demonstrate that using this method allows Majorana peaks to be clearly distinguished based on the presence of a characteristic 'V-shaped' conductance pattern.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as numerous different styles are applicable to these operations. Current machine learning-based methods typically disregard this stylistic variability in their pursuit of identifying a unique solution. Conversely, our research aims to harness style-specific information, extracting it from paired images to condense into a two or three-dimensional vector, resulting in a more efficient and understandable framework for style-based image editing. By representing the relationship between global color tones across paired images as a flow conditioned on the polynomial characteristics of the image pixels, our technique proves superior to other low-dimensional encoding methods, ultimately producing accurate re creations of the original image pair and the graded results, also achieving a notable increase in the variety of styles achievable through our technique.

This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC task, recently introduced in the LOVEU dataset, which is designed to evaluate multi-modal understanding of interactions within groups. The proposed framework leverages multi-modal fusion and graph attention mechanisms to analyze contextual cues and individual characteristics, ultimately enabling the detection of interactions among group members. The winning model achieved exceptional performance on the LOVEU dataset, with a remarkable top-1 accuracy of 72.6%, highlighting its effectiveness in the proposed framework.

This research focuses on the dynamics of snow falling in the atmosphere, using high-resolution simulations to analyze its behavior. Unlike other particles, snow particles are observed to settle in a specific direction vertical to their initial movement, a phenomenon known as preferential sweeping. To understand this phenomenon, the authors use a tool that identifies the tendency of particles to move alongside other particles of similar characteristics. They then demonstrate that strong attractions between particles of the same type cause a concentration effect, leading to a different settling direction. A theoretical model based on the ideas of a fluid with a memory function and a specific ratio of a particle's size to its surrounding distance is also developed to explain the concentration effect, and the resulting predictions accurately match the observed concentrations in the simulations. This study reveals that the speed at which particles settle is directly affected by their overall size and the strength of their inter-attractions, while their shape plays a less important role in this process. The findings of this research may also be applied to similar systems, such as atmospheric dust and pollen settling patterns.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data, such as video feeds, without the need for pre-defined parameters. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that such frameworks can be utilized to facilitate active inference. This study marks the first instance of applying active inference using deep learning techniques to a real-world navigation task involving a robotic system.

In experimental facilities specializing in high energy physics, nuclear physics, and cosmology, the task of processing large amounts of data in real-time is proving to be a substantial hurdle. As an alternative to standard compression methods, the use of machine learning algorithms has gained attention for real-time data reduction. Yet, data sets generated from scientific endeavors often comprise vast 3D data volumes characterized by significant portions of zeroes, non-uniform distribution of values, and high generation rates. Consequently, direct applications of popular compression methods along with standard compression methods fail to yield satisfactory results. Therefore, to overcome these complications, the concept of Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE) is developed to tackle the challenges posed by the unique properties of these data volumes by addressing both regression and sparsity simultaneously through the utilization of a dual-head autoencoder architecture. Through experiments, the superiority of BCAE has been established over traditional data compression methods in terms of data preservation fidelity and achievable compression ratio. Moreover, the efficacy of BCAE has been supported by an in-depth study, which revealed the importance of utilizing a dedicated decoder that specializes in data segmentation in order to further enhance reconstruction quality.

Utilizing Finzi's gravity theory that enhances interactions at large scales, we analyze galaxy clusters from a thermodynamic perspective, establishing a statistical model to derive thermodynamic equations and comparing clustering behavior with Newtonian gravity. We also explore the general distribution function's behavior as the clustering parameter varies in strength, with the finding that phase transitions are feasible, albeit hierarchically organized.

A type of convex geometric hypergraph, known as cgh, comprises a set of subsets originating from strictly convex point sets in the plane. In this study, researchers explore a specific type of problem associated with cghs: saturation problems that correspond to earlier studied extremal issues. Using a mathematical approach, the study determines the maximum capacity of certain geometrically separated groups of points and establishes an exact value for a specific instance, as well as approximate values for seven out of eight possible geometric hypergraph configurations up to a specific level of accuracy, and a related but less accurate figure for the eighth configuration.

To gain a better understanding of the relative contributions of different processes, the angular distributions and energy spectra of $\alpha$ and deuterons resulting from breakup, transfer, and incomplete fusion have been measured and calculated. Cross-sections for the $^6$Li + $^{51}$V system were experimentally measured at energies near the Coulomb barrier, with theoretical estimates obtained through calculations with the finite range coupled reaction method using the \textsc{FRESCO} code. Calculations indicated that the cross-sections from various reaction channels including non-capture breakup and 1 proton, 1 neutron, and 1 deuteron transfer, compound nuclear decay, and incomplete fusion channels can effectively reproduce both the direct $\alpha$ production cross-sections and their angular distributions. Furthermore, the observed direct $\alpha$ production cross-sections align with theoretical estimates, with significant predominance of $\sigma_\mathrm{H}$ (relative atomic mass greater than or equal to 12) over $\sigma_\mathrm{L}$ (relative atomic mass less than 12) at energies below the Coulomb barrier, with this trend reversed at energies above the Coulomb barrier.

A previously overlooked ability in bio-inspired snake robots is dynamic vertical climbing. A novel locomotion technique mimicking the Pacific Lamprey's movement has been discovered, which enables a robot to navigate on flat surfaces while climbing at near-vertical inclines. A simplified model has been created to analyze the correlation between robot motion and actuation, resulting in the development of a new, adaptable robot inspired by the Pacific Lamprey. The new robot, called Trident, successfully demonstrates dynamic vertical climbing at speeds of up to 4.8 cm/s and can also move horizontally at 9 cm/s. Furthermore, its climbing strides can be 14% longer than the Pacific Lamprey's, making this innovative design a promising approach for robots navigating steep surfaces with limited support points.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework.

Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success relies heavily on minimizing excessive interference through effective device scheduling. Traditional scheduling methods mainly prioritize maximizing throughput and fairness without considering the timeliness of received data. This paper presents a novel D2D link scheduling strategy that balances both Age of Information (AoI) and throughput by employing a packet replacement policy, which ensures fair link activation. Furthermore, a neural network-based approach is developed to solve the non-convex AoI optimization problem, yielding better performance than conventional methods like fractional routing and the alternative approach. The proposed solution is shown to outperform benchmark strategies in both fixed and dynamic D2D scenarios.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [25] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic, compressible flow with smooth solutions. This paper demonstrates that weak solutions to this system in a specific mathematical space ensure the conservation of helicity. Additionally, similar results were found for both homogeneous incompressible Euler equations and the surface quasi-geostrophic equation.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations, focusing particularly on the large spectral parameter $k$ in a specified reference \cite{KlSjSt20}. They now examined how this work can be applied to the reflection coefficient and derived new asymptotic formulas for specific domains with potential functions and smooth, strictly convex boundaries.

Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of merging compact binary systems,
including higher-order effects of gravitational wave radiation, reveal that late-time
eccentricities of inspiraling binaries are typically underestimated by standard
models by up to 30 percent for heavy systems like 300-solar-mass binaries at
10 Hz, and less so for lighter binaries. By incorporating more refined equations,
a novel, accurate analytic formula for eccentricities at late times is formulated.
Furthermore, this model's results remain largely insensitive to the masses of the
binary components, with a deviation of less than 5% from the predicted
eccentricities using standard models.

We're proposing the development of a highly intense, fully coherent X-ray
ampliconer using a combination of undulators and slotted micro-channel plates.
The device would be powered by the output of a free-electron laser oscillator and
would have numerous applications in the fields of nonlinear optics and
x-ray-based radiation-sourced science. The X-ray amplifier would be capable of
producing record-breaking levels of electromagnetic energy near the peak of the
X-ray spectrum, potentially exceeding 10 GW and lasting for nanosecond-scale
 durations, all while maintaining its fully coherent properties.

Event identification is crucial for informed decision-making in graph data analysis systems.  Graph-based machine learning has made notable advancements lately, but there is a notable absence of a unified framework for event detection on dynamic graphs, which are represented by time-stamped networks with evolving node and edge structures.  To bridge this gap, we introduce the concept of an event a node or edge involves the emergence of novel connections or the transformation of existing ones.  We propose the Dual-Time Graph Attention Network (DT-GAN) to recognize these events by monitoring the temporal and spatial interactions within a graph.  DT-GAN achieves state-of-the-art results on various datasets, outperforming existing methods by accurately modeling the non-linear relationships inherent in node and edge temporal dynamics.  Furthermore, we illustrate the effectiveness of DT-GAN on real-world datasets by pinpointing significant events like the ascent of Wikipedia pages and the uncovering of the Russian intelligence operation during the 2016 US presidential election.

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent. Moreover, we show that when the density exponent is not a perfect integer, the solutions exhibit oscillatory behavior before eventually converging to the uniform density case, featuring a singular behavior at the origin.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization.

In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. We establish a comprehensive single-letter representation of the optimal normalized leakage in this adversarial scenario, along with a stochastic coding method that reaches this optimum. Interestingly, our analysis shows that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates are attainable by certain deterministic coding strategies, where these goals can be concurrently achieved. We expand upon the initial investigation to consider adversaries that submit multiple guesses and can tolerate a degree of sequence error. In this case, we identify tight lower and upper bounds for the more general leakage metric through the application of single-letter analysis.

Deep learning-trained generative models can function as a prior in under-determined inverse problems such as generating images from limited measurements, like a few pixels, by utilizing the generated lower-resolution image as a prior. We trained a generative model on SAR data, specifically using the VHR-1 dataset, to improve the resolution of 10m × 10m areas from 1m × 1m data, a factor of 10 improvement, and found that previous models were unable to provide significant improvement. We developed a new hierarchical generative model to address this issue. The first level generates a scene summary and the second level uses the generated map to produce a high-resolution image. We used an encoder-decoder architecture with a residual block and trained it using a self-supervised sample-specific adaptive regularization loss function. The model performed satisfactorily in a complementary evaluation, but directly applying it to use the generated low-resolution image as a prior was ineffective. We modified the model to work with real-world data collected by an airborne system, specifically Geosystems Chicago's P-band collection, which features a 30m × 30m resolution and a 10m × 10m sparse sample. We used two distinct datasets: the VHR dataset and the P-band dataset, to evaluate our model's effectiveness. We demonstrated the model's ability to improve the resolution of 10m × 10m areas from 1m × 1m data across various scenarios and found our hierarchical generative

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative global optimizers.  The proposed technique leads to considerable reductions in circuit access frequency, typically the costliest QAOA component.  The framework performs well even at slow circuit repetition rates and with minimal quantum circuit measurements, yielding a reliable energy estimate.  Moreover, we investigate how our approach handles noise during circuit operation, discovering that for short circuits it remains resistant to disturbances.  The outcome of these findings supports the use of the suggested method as an adaptable tool to exploit the mixed capabilities of QAOA within imperfect quantum devices.

A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computational power within a computer program as the union of the overlap region and the difference between the two ellipses can be identified using simple mathematical operations. The Gauss node evaluation routine, used for placing nodes within the union region in order to calculate the overlap area through integration, has been adapted for this purpose. The approach has been further generalized for determining the overlap area between elliptical sectors for greater efficiency. The proposed method has been thoroughly validated against a numerical integration technique and the results indicate perfect agreement in the exact arithmetic mode, while the relative error in the approximate arithmetic mode is less than 10 to the power of negative 9. The proposed method has been demonstrated to determine the overlap area between two ellipses within a millisecond for a thousand iterations with N up to 20, n up to 20 and both a and b up to 10.0, indicating its suitability for a wide range of applications. The approach has been further generalized for placing nodes inside the union region of two elliptical sectors and the overlap area between these regions can be calculated through integration. The proposed method has been validated against a numerical integration technique and the results indicate perfect agreement in the exact arithmetic mode, while the relative error in the approximate arithmetic mode is less than 10 to the power of negative 9.
